The release arrives as DeepSeek begins preparations for a potential initial public offering on Shanghai’s technology-focused STAR Market, according to earlier Reuters reporting. That connection puts the technical launch in a wider race among Chinese AI developers to fund computing capacity, win users and build domestic alternatives to U.S.-based model providers.

The practical test will be whether developers see consistent gains across real workloads, not only company demonstrations. Until technical documentation and outside evaluations are available, DeepSeek’s performance claims should be treated as the maker’s description. The Flash branding suggests an emphasis on efficiency and response speed within the broader V4.1 family.
dek: The Chinese AI startup says the release is designed for faster inference and higher throughput while supporting larger models in the same architecture.
headline: DeepSeek launches V4.1-Flash as smallest model in new AI family

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Germany’s military is evaluating 30 artificial-intelligence tools intended to speed battlefield decision-making, with an initial system targeted for introduction beginning in 2027, Reuters reported Thursday.

Vice Admiral Thomas Daum, head of the military’s cyber command, told Handelsblatt that he was optimistic a prototype would be available in the second quarter of 2027. Full implementation is expected in 2028. Most products under review come from German companies, while France’s ChapsVision is among the foreign participants.

Modern drones and satellites generate large volumes of imagery and other data that can overwhelm human analysts. The military is examining whether AI can organize that information quickly enough to improve situational awareness while commanders retain responsibility for operational decisions.

The review also reflects European concerns about data control and dependence on overseas suppliers. Daum said in April that Germany was not then planning to buy Palantir’s Maven Smart System, which is used by the United States, NATO commands and several allies. The current evaluation does not guarantee any individual vendor a contract.
dek: Germany’s cyber-command chief said a prototype could be ready in the second quarter of 2027, with broader implementation targeted for 2028.
headline: German military evaluates 30 AI tools for battlefield decisions

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Large shareholder-return plans from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are testing South Korea’s effort to narrow the longstanding valuation gap between its companies and global peers.

Reuters reported that the two chipmakers’ payout plans are worth more than 130 trillion won, about $97 billion, for 2026. Strong demand tied to artificial intelligence has boosted cash generation and increased investor pressure for dividends and share buybacks.

Investors welcomed the planned distributions but said broader changes in governance, capital allocation and shareholder rights are still needed. Samsung faces particular calls to put more emphasis on repurchasing shares rather than relying mainly on dividends.

At the time of the Reuters report, the benchmark KOSPI remained about 26% below the record it reached in June, even though Samsung and SK Hynix account for nearly half of the index’s weight. That percentage is a dated market measure, not a live quotation. The muted response illustrates why South Korea’s reform program will be judged across many companies and over time, not by two large payouts alone.
dek: The chipmakers’ combined 2026 shareholder-return plans exceed 130 trillion won, but investors say governance and capital-allocation concerns remain.
headline: Samsung and SK Hynix payouts test South Korea’s market reforms

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Foreign investors returned to net buying of Asian equities in August after nine consecutive months of selling, Reuters reported using LSEG market-flow data.

Investors purchased a net $4.72 billion of shares in Taiwan, South Korea, India, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines during the month. They added another $1.52 billion through Tuesday’s close in September. Those figures are historical snapshots and do not represent live flows.

The shift was concentrated around technology exporters linked to artificial-intelligence spending. Taiwan received $11.15 billion of net inflows in August, while South Korea still recorded an $8.65 billion outflow for a fourth consecutive month. Early September data showed foreign buying returning to both markets.

Corporate results helped improve sentiment: Asian companies beat analyst earnings estimates by an average 10.2% in the latest quarter, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. Profit growth was 44.7% from a year earlier across the sample, with technology growth at 88.3%. The concentration suggests renewed AI exposure, rather than a uniform return to every Asian market.
dek: LSEG data showed $4.72 billion of net purchases across seven Asian markets in August, led by renewed interest in AI-linked exporters.
headline: Foreign investors return to Asian stocks after nine-month selloff

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown left Wednesday night’s season opener in Seattle with a right ankle injury during the third quarter.

Brown was targeted by quarterback Drake Maye on third down when Seahawks nickel cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett deflected the pass. Pritchett’s knee landed on the outside of Brown’s ankle as the receiver went to the turf, Reuters reported. Brown walked off, removed his right cleat and entered the sideline medical tent.

The Patriots initially listed him as questionable to return. He did not rejoin the offense when a roughing-the-punter penalty extended the possession. Brown had three receptions for a team-high 26 yards in the first half.

New England acquired Brown from the Philadelphia Eagles in an early-June trade, making his availability an important early-season issue for the passing game. The initial report did not include a diagnosis, imaging result or recovery timeline. Any assessment beyond a right ankle injury would therefore be premature until the team provides a medical update.
dek: Brown walked off during New England’s first possession of the second half in Seattle and was initially listed as questionable to return.
headline: Patriots receiver A.J. Brown leaves opener with right ankle injury

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Barry Melrose, a former NHL player and coach who became one of ESPN’s most recognizable hockey analysts, died Wednesday at age 70, the network announced.

Melrose spent 27 years with ESPN and became known for direct commentary, deep familiarity with the sport and a distinctive on-air appearance. He left the network in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.

Before broadcasting, Melrose coached the Los Angeles Kings for more than two seasons and led the Wayne Gretzky-captained team to the 1993 Stanley Cup Final. A brief later stint with the Tampa Bay Lightning brought his NHL head-coaching record to 84-108-29-4.

The Saskatchewan native also played nine professional seasons as a defenseman. He appeared in the World Hockey Association with Cincinnati and later played 300 NHL games for Winnipeg, Toronto and Detroit. ESPN described him as a foundational figure in its hockey coverage. His death is significant across the sport, including in New England, where ESPN’s Bristol studios helped make his analysis a familiar part of national NHL broadcasts.
dek: The longtime broadcaster, known for an unmistakable style and direct analysis, spent 27 years covering hockey for ESPN.
headline: Former NHL coach and ESPN analyst Barry Melrose dies at 70

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A University of New Hampshire-led aquaculture project is producing about 20,000 pounds of steelhead trout at a floating research facility off Portsmouth, offering a local test of how offshore fish farming could increase the domestic seafood supply.

Boston 25 News reported that the roughly 50-by-30-foot facility is operated by UNH’s Center for Sustainable Seafood Systems. The fish begin their lives at an inland site in New Hampshire’s Lakes Region before being transferred to salt water and raised offshore. Harvest typically comes when each fish reaches about five or six pounds.

The operation also grows mussels, kelp and other seaweed around the fish. Those species can absorb nutrients released by the farm, while researchers monitor the surrounding water to measure environmental effects and refine the system. The work is intended to test production methods rather than assume that every coastal site will perform the same way.

UNH was selected for a broader federal effort to develop sustainable aquaculture in several U.S. regions. Related work is underway in Alabama, with projects planned for Hawaii and California. For New Hampshire, the Portsmouth farm links marine science, food production and the region’s long-running effort to build a resilient coastal economy.
dek: A floating research facility off the New Hampshire coast is testing whether domestic seafood production can expand while monitoring water quality and managing nutrients.
headline: UNH offshore fish farm raises 20,000 pounds of steelhead near Portsmouth

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Microscopic life on the Gulf of Maine seafloor is changing as native kelp forests retreat and invasive red turf algae spread, according to research highlighted by New Hampshire Public Radio and Maine Public.

Scientists from the University of Maine and Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences examined microbial communities associated with the region’s changing underwater habitat. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, connects the shift to a Gulf that is warming rapidly and becoming less favorable for some native kelp.

Kelp is a foundational species: its underwater forests provide structure, food and shelter for a wide range of marine life. When low-growing turf algae replace it, the visible habitat changes and so do the bacteria and other microbes living around it. Those organisms help cycle nutrients and can influence whether an ecosystem resists disruption or recovers afterward.

Researchers said the long-term consequences are not yet clear, making continued monitoring important. The findings matter along New Hampshire’s short coastline because the Gulf functions as one connected system. Changes first detected on the ocean floor can ultimately affect fisheries, water quality and coastal communities that depend on a healthy marine food web.
dek: Researchers found that warming waters and the spread of invasive turf algae are changing microscopic communities on the seafloor, with uncertain effects on ecosystem recovery.
headline: Gulf of Maine study tracks microbial shifts as kelp forests retreat

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Authorities are investigating a homicide in Salem after a 42-year-old woman was found dead inside a Cabot Street residence during a well-being check Wednesday morning.

Boston 25 News reported that Salem police responded at about 11:30 a.m. and discovered the woman’s body. Officials had not released her name in the initial report. The Essex County District Attorney’s Office and Salem police are handling the investigation, and no additional circumstances surrounding the death were immediately disclosed.

A 50-year-old Salem man was arrested later in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, on a warrant connected to the case. He was expected to appear first in New Hampshire as a fugitive from justice before being returned to Massachusetts. Prosecutors said he would then be arraigned in Salem District Court on a murder charge.

The charge is an allegation, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. Authorities said they expected to release more information Thursday. The arrest also adds a cross-state legal step before the Massachusetts case can proceed, with New Hampshire authorities responsible for the initial fugitive proceeding and transfer process.
dek: A 50-year-old Salem man was taken into custody in New Hampshire after police found a 42-year-old woman dead during a well-being check on Cabot Street.
headline: Salem homicide suspect arrested in Portsmouth after woman found dead

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts drivers were paying an average of about $4.24 a gallon for regular gasoline Wednesday, according to AAA figures cited by Boston 25 News, as another rise in crude oil intensified concern about household and business costs.

The station reported that oil gained more than 3% during Wednesday’s session. The national gasoline average was about $4.22, compared with roughly $3.19 a year earlier. The Massachusetts figure was described as a record for this point in the calendar. These numbers reflect the source’s Wednesday snapshot and should not be read as live prices.

The impact extends beyond fuel pumps. Diesel prices feed into trucking and delivery costs, while heating oil remains an important winter expense for many New England households. Sustained increases can reach grocery shelves and service bills as companies pass along higher transportation and operating costs.

Day-to-day prices can move quickly with crude markets, refinery conditions, regional inventories and distribution constraints. The latest increase therefore does not establish where costs will settle for the heating season. It does, however, sharpen the region’s affordability concerns just as residents and fuel suppliers begin preparing for colder weather.
dek: AAA figures cited Wednesday put regular gasoline near a seasonal record, while higher crude prices renewed concern about diesel, heating oil and transportation costs.
headline: Massachusetts gas average reaches about $4.24 as oil rally raises winter concerns

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: U.S. Sen. Jack Reed won Rhode Island’s Democratic Senate primary, according to results published by the Rhode Island Board of Elections after Wednesday’s voting.

Reed faced challenger Connor Burbridge for the nomination. The state results page showed Reed advancing, while election officials continued the routine canvass and certification process. Published election-night totals are unofficial until that work is complete, including review of eligible mail ballots and any provisional ballots.

The outcome places Reed on the November ballot alongside Republican nominee Raymond McKay and independent candidate Michael Bahry. The general election will determine who represents Rhode Island in the six-year Senate term beginning in January. This article reports the primary result and does not assess or predict the general-election contest.

The Senate race was one of several statewide and municipal contests on Rhode Island’s primary ballot. With nominations now largely settled, candidates move into a shorter fall campaign in which federal policy, household costs and local priorities are expected to remain prominent. Voters can use the Board of Elections results portal for updated totals and official certification information.
dek: Official state results showed the incumbent advancing from Wednesday’s primary, setting the U.S. Senate field for the November general election.
headline: Jack Reed wins Rhode Island Democratic U.S. Senate primary

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island’s Republican primary for governor remained too close to call Thursday morning, with Aaron Guckian and Elaine Pelino separated by only a few hundred votes after most ballots had been counted, according to the Associated Press.

Guckian entered the contest with the state Republican Party’s endorsement, while Pelino also sought the nomination to challenge for the open governorship. The narrow margin means the race depends on completion of the official count, including eligible mail and provisional ballots, rather than an election-night projection.

No winner should be inferred until election officials complete the canvass and the margin is clear under Rhode Island law. The Board of Elections publishes updated unofficial totals and later certifies results. Any recount procedures would depend on the final certified margin and applicable state rules.

The eventual Republican nominee is expected to face Democratic nominee Helena Foulkes and independent candidate Ken Block in November. This is a status report on the unresolved primary, not a forecast of either the nomination or general election. The next meaningful update will come from verified state totals or an official call based on those results.
dek: Aaron Guckian and Elaine Pelino were separated by only a few hundred votes Thursday morning, leaving the GOP nomination unresolved while ballots are reviewed.
headline: Rhode Island Republican governor primary remains too close to call

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Russian strike hit a petrol station complex in southwestern Kyiv early Thursday, injuring four people and setting off fires, Ukrainian officials said.

Reuters reported that the attack marked the first time a petrol station had been struck in the Ukrainian capital during the war. Images from the scene showed heavy damage, including at least one destroyed vehicle. Fire also spread to a neighboring building before emergency crews worked to contain it.

The strike came during another night of drone attacks on Kyiv. The city has faced an almost continuous barrage of jet-powered drones for nearly two weeks, increasing pressure on air defenses and emergency services. Officials were still assessing the full damage and did not immediately provide detailed information about the condition of those injured.

Claims and casualty figures in an active conflict can change as responders search damaged areas and authorities verify reports. The core facts in this article are attributed to Ukrainian officials and Reuters reporting available Thursday morning. The attack remains a developing story, with additional information expected from Kyiv’s emergency and military authorities.
dek: Emergency crews responded after an overnight attack ignited a fuel complex in southwestern Kyiv, as the city endured another wave of Russian drones.
headline: Russian strike hits Kyiv petrol station and injures four

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Hong Kong court convicted Dow Jones, publisher of The Wall Street Journal, of willfully preventing former reporter Selina Cheng from exercising her right to become an officer of a trade union.

Reuters reported that the case was brought under Hong Kong’s Trade Unions Ordinance. The court found against the company on the union-rights charge but acquitted it of unlawfully dismissing Cheng, ruling that prosecutors had not excluded the company’s restructuring explanation beyond a reasonable doubt.

Cheng was elected chair of the Hong Kong Journalists Association in 2024. The case has drawn attention because it tests legal protections for labor organizing within an international news organization at a time of heightened concern about media freedom in Hong Kong.

Dow Jones said it disagreed with the conviction and was evaluating its next steps. Each charge carries a maximum fine of HK$100,000, and sentencing was expected later. The mixed verdict leaves both the labor-rights finding and the acquittal important: the court recognized an unlawful effort to block union participation while declining to find that the dismissal itself met the criminal standard.
dek: A court found the Wall Street Journal publisher unlawfully blocked former reporter Selina Cheng from becoming a union officer, while acquitting it on a separate dismissal charge.
headline: Hong Kong court convicts Dow Jones over reporter’s union bid

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: IBM and NASA released an open-source artificial-intelligence model Thursday that is designed to help scientists analyze decades of lunar observations and prepare for longer-term exploration of the Moon.

The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model was trained on more than 30 layers of data collected by nine instruments across four NASA missions, including the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. It joins the partners’ Prithvi family of foundation models for geospatial, weather and other scientific work.

Researchers can use the system to identify possible ice deposits in permanently shadowed regions, map craters that may affect landing safety and study volcanic features. IBM and NASA said benchmark tests showed accuracy improvements of as much as 23% over widely used methods for certain lunar features.

Water ice is especially important because it could support drinking water, oxygen production and rocket fuel for future missions. The model does not replace scientific review or mission planning, but it can help teams sort large volumes of observation data more efficiently. NASA’s Artemis program currently plans to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028 as part of preparations for sustained lunar operations and eventual Mars missions.
dek: The open-source Lunar Foundation Model combines data from four NASA missions to help researchers identify resources, landing hazards and volcanic features.
headline: IBM and NASA launch AI model to map lunar ice and craters

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: AI chip startup d-Matrix said Thursday that its next-generation Raptor processors will use Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion technology, allowing the custom chips to connect directly inside Nvidia-compatible data-center systems.

D-Matrix focuses on inference, the stage when trained models power services such as coding assistants, chatbots and voice agents. Nvidia dominates the market for chips used to train large models, while NVLink Fusion gives outside processor designers access to specialized links and memory connections within its broader server architecture.

The Raptor chips are scheduled to complete final design by the end of 2026, and compatible server racks are expected in 2027. D-Matrix is also working with Astera Labs on high-speed data movement across the system. Financial terms of the Nvidia collaboration were not disclosed.

The Santa Clara company shipped its first AI chip in November 2024 and was valued at $2 billion after raising $450 million in 2025. Microsoft has backed the startup since an earlier financing round. The partnership shows how smaller chipmakers are seeking a route into established data-center platforms as demand shifts from building models toward running them quickly and efficiently at scale.
dek: The startup’s upcoming Raptor processors will connect directly to Nvidia data-center systems through NVLink Fusion, with compatible racks expected in 2027.
headline: D-Matrix adopts Nvidia chip-linking tech for AI inference servers

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Oil prices climbed about 4% Thursday as a surge in attacks on shipping intensified concern that supplies could be disrupted through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.

At 12:15 p.m. GMT, Reuters reported Brent crude futures up $4.05 at $105.26 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose $3.99 to $100.04, moving above $100 for the first time since May. Those figures are a dated market snapshot, not live prices.

Brent has risen more than 30% from early-August lows as a lasting halt to U.S.-Iran attacks failed to take hold. Iran-aligned Houthi forces seized Yemen’s port of Mocha on Thursday, according to military sources, adding risk near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait while Gulf traffic through Hormuz remained restricted.

Oil prices can reverse quickly as traders reassess military events, shipping access, inventories and demand. The immediate move nevertheless matters for New England because higher crude costs can filter into gasoline, diesel and heating oil. It also complicates the inflation outlook facing central banks and consumers ahead of the Northern Hemisphere winter.
dek: Brent gained about 4% in a Thursday midday snapshot as attacks and restricted shipping raised fears of disruption through two major energy corridors.
headline: Oil jumps to $105 as Middle East tanker attacks escalate

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The European Union’s securities regulator warned Thursday that upbeat asset valuations are increasingly disconnected from a weakening economic outlook, raising the risk of an abrupt market correction.

Reuters reported that European Securities and Markets Authority Chair Verena Ross cited geopolitical tension and rising energy prices among the pressures testing investor confidence. ESMA also described operational risk as very high and increasing, in part because advances in artificial intelligence can help attackers find and exploit cyber vulnerabilities.

The regulator repeated concerns that shocks in crypto markets could spread more widely as links with traditional finance grow. Tokenized equities remain a very small share of global markets, but ESMA said wider adoption could alter market structure. It also highlighted manipulation and insider-trading risks in fast-growing prediction markets that allow wagers on elections, wars and sports.

A regulatory warning is not a forecast that a selloff will occur, and it does not set a timeline. It identifies channels through which losses or operational failures could spread if sentiment changes suddenly. For investors, the report adds a cautionary counterweight to high valuations at a time when energy costs, interest rates and geopolitical events are moving together.
dek: ESMA said weakening economic signals, geopolitical stress and elevated asset prices are widening a gap that leaves markets vulnerable to a sharp reversal.
headline: EU watchdog warns optimistic valuations could trigger abrupt market correction

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The New York Mets survived the loss of an eight-run lead and beat the Miami Marlins 15-14 on Wednesday night, completing a three-game road sweep in one of the season’s most volatile games.

New York led 8-0 in the third inning before Miami scored three times in the fourth and five in the sixth to tie the game. The Mets answered with six runs in the seventh, highlighted by Francisco Lindor’s three-run homer and Christopher Morel’s run-scoring single.

Morel finished 3-for-4 with three RBIs as the Mets extended their winning streak to four games. Miami continued to pressure the bullpen, but Tobias Myers recorded the final two outs for his second save and preserved the one-run margin.

The result improved New York’s run to 21-12 since the club sold at the trade deadline, according to Reuters. A 15-14 score can obscure how dramatically control shifted: the Mets built what appeared to be a comfortable advantage, surrendered all of it, then produced another major rally. The win mattered in the standings, but it also tested a reshaped roster’s ability to finish a game after momentum had fully reversed.
dek: New York recovered after Miami erased an 8-0 deficit, scoring six times in the seventh inning to complete a three-game sweep.
headline: Mets survive blown eight-run lead to beat Marlins 15-14

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe will meet Friday in the first Grand Slam semifinal between two Black American men in the Open Era, adding a historic milestone to the U.S. Open.

The matchup guarantees an American finalist and follows separate quarterfinal victories that moved both players within one win of the championship round. Shelton and Tiafoe have shared Arthur Ashe Stadium before: they met in the 2023 U.S. Open quarterfinals, giving Friday’s contest a recent competitive history as well as broader significance.

Tiafoe also reached the U.S. Open semifinals in 2024. Shelton has since added major hard-court credentials, including two Masters 1000 titles and a victory in Montreal in August 2026. Their progress reflects a deeper group of American men contending late at major tournaments.

The tournament also has an important parallel in the women’s draw, where Coco Gauff advanced to the semifinals after rallying past Mirra Andreeva. The Shelton-Tiafoe match should be judged on tactics and form, but its place in tennis history is already established: for the first time in the Open Era, two Black American men will share a major semifinal stage.
dek: Friday’s U.S. Open matchup will be the first Open Era Grand Slam semifinal between two Black American men, guaranteeing a home finalist.
headline: Shelton-Tiafoe semifinal makes Grand Slam history for Black American men

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Southern New Hampshire’s September 10–13 calendar includes community festivals, museum programming, live music, food events and artisan markets across Manchester, Nashua, Concord and several surrounding towns.

Manchester’s Latino Vibe Festival is scheduled for Saturday from noon to 9 p.m. at Veterans Memorial Park, with live bands and free admission. The Currier Museum of Art will hold Community Day from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., pairing its Radical Quiet exhibition with activities involving the Society for the Protection of New Hampshire Forests and opportunities to meet featured artists.

Other Saturday options include the Wags to Whiskers Festival at Holman Stadium in Nashua, Arts in the Park at Rollins Park in Concord and the Wicked Wine & Brewfest in Litchfield. Multi-day events include Nashua’s Egyptian Food Festival, Manchester’s St. Pius X Parish Fair and the River Valley Artisans Art & Wine Festival in Westmoreland.

The lineup begins Thursday with smaller library, skating and live-music programs and continues through Sunday with Cars & Coffee on Capitol in Concord. Organizers and the Manchester Ink Link guide advise visitors to check venue information for admission requirements and last-minute changes before traveling.
dek: A busy September 10–13 calendar includes Manchester’s Latino Vibe Festival, Community Day at the Currier and events from Nashua to Westmoreland.
headline: Southern New Hampshire weekend slate spans festivals, art and live music

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Nashua South remained unbeaten Wednesday with a 2-1 boys soccer victory over Manchester Memorial, moving the Purple Panthers to 4-0 early in the season.

Kevin Araujo shaped both South goals. Sixteen minutes into the match, his corner kick found senior Max Friday for a header and a 1-0 lead. Manchester Memorial answered nine minutes later when Leis Taric chased down a long ball and scored in his season debut.

South regained the advantage four minutes into the second half. A clearance created a one-on-one opportunity for Araujo, who beat the defender with his speed and finished low for his first goal of the season. Memorial increased its pressure afterward, but South protected the one-goal margin through the final whistle.

South coach Tom Bellen told Manchester Ink Link that the result came despite a performance below the team’s preferred level, while Memorial coach Jerold White pointed to quicker decisions with the ball as an area to improve. The close match offered both teams an early-season test: Nashua South showed it could win without its best performance, and Memorial stayed within one play of an undefeated opponent.
dek: Kevin Araujo assisted on the opening goal and scored the winner as the Purple Panthers improved to 4-0.
headline: Nashua South boys soccer stays unbeaten with 2-1 win over Manchester Memorial

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: An MBTA bus was involved in a multi-vehicle crash on the Fellsway in Medford on Thursday morning, prompting a large emergency response and sending the bus driver to a hospital.

WHDH reported that several vehicles were involved and that the collision knocked down a pole. A person near the scene told the station she could see the driver through a window and believed the driver appeared unconscious. Emergency crews later transported the driver for medical care.

Officials had not released the driver’s condition, the number of other people injured or the circumstances leading to the crash when the initial report was published. The MBTA bus route involved also was not immediately identified.

The collision could affect traffic while investigators document the scene and crews address the damaged pole and vehicles. Drivers using the Fellsway should expect possible delays and follow local police directions. Because the response remained active, early details may change as Medford police, fire officials and the MBTA provide additional information. The cause of the crash remains under investigation, and no conclusion about fault has been announced.
dek: Several vehicles were involved in the Thursday morning collision on the Fellsway, where a utility pole was knocked down.
headline: MBTA bus crash in Medford sends driver to hospital

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A man accused in a May shooting along Memorial Drive in Cambridge is expected to appear in court in person for the first time while facing dozens of newly filed charges.

WHDH identified the defendant as 47-year-old Tyler Brown. The station reported that the new counts include six charges of armed assault to murder, seven charges of malicious damage to a motor vehicle, carrying a firearm without a license and possessing a firearm after a felony conviction.

Prosecutors allege Brown fired dozens of rounds from a rifle at drivers along Memorial Drive. Two people were struck and later recovered. Brown’s earlier court appearance took place by video from a hospital bed, according to the report.

The charges are allegations, and Brown is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. His upcoming appearance advances a case that has been developing for nearly four months and will allow the court to address the expanded charging document. WHDH also reported that Brown was on parole at the time in connection with a 2020 shooting involving Boston police officers. Any plea, bail decision or schedule for further proceedings will be determined in court.
dek: Tyler Brown is expected to appear in person as prosecutors add armed-assault, firearm and property-damage counts tied to the May shooting.
headline: Memorial Drive shooting suspect faces dozens of new charges

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: One person died and two others were taken to Rhode Island Hospital after a vehicle crashed and caught fire on West Main Road in Middletown early Thursday, police said.
Officers responded at about 1:20 a.m. to the area near Linden Park. Investigators said the vehicle was traveling south when it struck a stone wall and a utility pole, then ignited.

First responders removed the driver and a front-seat passenger and transported both to the hospital. A passenger in the back seat could not be removed and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to NBC 10 WJAR’s report on the police investigation.

Authorities had not released the names of the occupants or the conditions of the two survivors when the report was published. Police also had not announced what may have caused the vehicle to leave the road. The crash remains under investigation. Residents and drivers in the area should follow any temporary traffic controls while investigators and utility crews complete their work near the damaged pole. Further information is expected after notifications and the initial reconstruction are complete.
dek: Police say a southbound vehicle hit a stone wall and utility pole before catching fire near Linden Park early Thursday.
headline: Middletown crash kills back-seat passenger, sends two to hospital

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Roger Williams Park Zoo is mourning Zipper, a 27-year-old zebra that was euthanized after suffering a critical wound believed to have been caused by another animal in her habitat.

The zoo’s animal-care, veterinary and operations teams arranged for a large-animal surgical and anesthesia team from Tufts University to assist with emergency treatment. After evaluating the injury, the teams determined it was not survivable, according to a report by NBC 10 WJAR.
Staff remembered Zipper as a confident, familiar presence with a strong interest in carrots. She had spent 27 years at the Providence zoo and was well known to employees and visitors.

The loss also creates an immediate animal-care concern for Tundra, the zoo’s remaining zebra. Staff said Tundra was closely attached to Zipper and often waited for her before going inside or eating. Because zebras are herd animals, the zoo is monitoring Tundra and working to bring in new companions. The care team is also reviewing what happened and considering changes intended to reduce the risk of a similar injury. No further details about the other animal or the precise circumstances of the wound were released in the initial account.
dek: Veterinary teams determined the 27-year-old zebra’s wound was not survivable; the zoo is monitoring her longtime companion and reviewing the incident.
headline: Roger Williams Park Zoo mourns Zipper the zebra after critical injury

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Twenty-five people died Thursday in a fire aboard a cargo vessel undergoing repairs at a state-owned shipyard in Qingdao, eastern China, state media reported.

The fire began at about 11:15 a.m. local time during repair and inspection work at the Qingdao Beihai shipyard. Of 42 people aboard, 12 were evacuated safely and five were injured and hospitalized, according to Xinhua figures reported by Reuters. Firefighters extinguished the blaze by early afternoon.

Images identified the vessel as the Ocean Melody. LSEG ship-tracking data described it as a 20-year-old, Liberia-flagged dry bulk carrier that arrived at the yard on August 31 and remained there for repairs.

China’s leadership called for intensified rescue work, a rapid investigation and accountability measures. The shipyard is controlled by China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a major state-owned shipbuilder. The cause of the fire had not been announced. Investigators will need to establish where the blaze started, what work was underway and whether fire-control systems and evacuation procedures operated as intended. The casualty count and investigation remain developing.
dek: The Ocean Melody was undergoing repairs when fire broke out Thursday; 12 people escaped and five were hospitalized.
headline: Cargo-ship fire at Qingdao shipyard kills 25

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: At least 24 children were killed when a fire tore through two schools and about 300 wooden homes in Bukavu, a city in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo controlled by AFC/M23 rebels, a local official said Thursday.

The dead included 19 girls and five boys, according to South Kivu’s vice governor in the rebel-appointed administration. Twenty-nine people were reported injured, although accounts from hospitals and residents indicated that the toll could change as officials reconcile casualties.
The fire was out by Thursday afternoon, but smoke continued to rise from rubble and twisted roofing, a Reuters witness reported. Investigators had not determined the cause.

Bukavu has been under the control of the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 movement since its rapid advance through eastern Congo in 2025. That conflict complicates public administration and emergency response in a densely populated city. The immediate priorities are identifying victims, treating the injured, sheltering families whose homes were destroyed and establishing how flames spread into school buildings. Officials and health workers cautioned that the death toll could rise, making this an active emergency with significant uncertainty around the final number of victims.
dek: Officials said 19 girls and five boys were among the dead as flames also destroyed roughly 300 wooden homes in the rebel-held city.
headline: Bukavu fire kills at least 24 children and destroys two schools

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The European Union’s cybersecurity agency has been granted access to two advanced artificial-intelligence models and has begun testing one of them, the European Commission said Thursday.

ENISA is testing Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and has also received access to OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, according to a Commission spokesperson quoted by Reuters. The brief announcement did not specify the test methods, timetable or results.

Access gives the agency an opportunity to examine how frontier systems behave in security-sensitive scenarios. That can include evaluating whether a model strengthens defensive analysis, generates risky technical guidance or resists attempts to bypass safeguards. Reuters’ report did not say that either model had failed a test or caused an incident.

The review comes as European regulators and security officials seek a clearer picture of rapidly improving model capabilities. Independent access matters because evaluations performed by public agencies can complement testing conducted by developers. ENISA’s findings could inform how institutions assess emerging cyber risks, but the Commission did not announce any enforcement action or policy change. Until results are released, the development is best understood as a new stage of official technical scrutiny rather than a judgment about either company’s model.
dek: ENISA has received access to Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra as European officials examine advanced models’ cyber capabilities.
headline: EU cybersecurity agency tests Anthropic and OpenAI frontier models

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Portuguese digital-rights group D3 has filed collective lawsuits against Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, alleging that platform features are designed to keep users engaged in harmful ways.

The four actions were filed in Lisbon Civil Court between April and May and disclosed after Portugal’s judicial summer break, D3 said Thursday. Collective actions allow an association to bring claims on behalf of a wider group of consumers.

D3 identified infinite scrolling, autoplay video, persistent notifications and highly personalized recommendations as features that remove natural stopping points and repeatedly draw users back. The group is seeking accountability and changes it says would create a safer experience.

Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet, the companies behind the named services, did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. The allegations have not been adjudicated. The cases join broader scrutiny of social-media design in Europe and the United States, including regulatory proceedings and civil claims concerning compulsive use. D3 said the four platforms together reached 33 million monthly users in Portugal during the first half of 2026, based on data aggregated by SocialMediaTransparency.org. The lawsuits now move into a court process that will test both the group’s claims and the companies’ defenses.
dek: Digital-rights organization D3 says infinite scrolling, autoplay and personalized recommendations create harmful feedback loops.
headline: Portuguese group sues Meta, TikTok and YouTube over addictive design

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The European Central Bank raised its benchmark deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on Thursday, delivering its second rate increase of 2026 as higher energy costs pushed eurozone inflation above target.

The ECB said risks were tilted toward higher inflation and weaker growth. It now expects average inflation of 3.0% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027, while lifting its 2026 growth projection slightly to 0.9% from 0.8%.

Oil and natural-gas prices have risen during the Iran war, creating pressure that policymakers are trying to prevent from spreading into wages and a wider range of goods and services. Underlying inflation slowed in the latest data, however, and wage growth has moderated, giving officials reasons to proceed carefully.

Financial markets had widely anticipated Thursday’s decision, so attention shifted to the timing of any follow-up move. Higher government-bond yields are already tightening financing conditions, which can slow demand independently of central-bank action. For investors and businesses, the key question is whether the energy shock remains concentrated in fuel costs or becomes persistent across the economy. The ECB did not commit to a preset path for rates.
dek: The European Central Bank delivered its second increase of 2026 and lifted its inflation forecast while warning that price risks remain tilted upward.
headline: ECB raises deposit rate to 2.5% as energy inflation accelerates

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: British government borrowing costs climbed to multi-decade highs Thursday as rising oil prices, firm U.S. inflation data and expectations for tighter monetary policy drove a broad bond-market selloff.

The 10-year gilt yield rose to 5.378%, its highest since July 2007, Reuters reported. Yields on 20- and 30-year debt reached 5.895% and 5.948%, respectively, their highest levels since 1998. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Shorter maturities also sold off. The five-year yield recorded its largest one-day increase since May 15 and reached a three-year high near 4.95%, while the two-year yield rose to its highest since October 2023.

The Bank of England is expected to hold rates at its next meeting, but futures markets moved toward a greater likelihood of an increase in November as energy costs added to inflation concerns. These figures describe Thursday’s market levels and are not live quotes. The jump matters beyond trading desks because government yields influence mortgage pricing, corporate borrowing and the cost of servicing public debt. Investors will be watching whether energy prices stabilize and whether incoming inflation data validate expectations for additional central-bank tightening.
dek: Ten-year borrowing costs touched levels last seen in 2007, while 20- and 30-year yields reached their highest points since 1998.
headline: UK bond yields reach multi-decade highs amid global selloff

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover, who commanded and piloted the Artemis II flight around the moon in April, are stepping away from active astronaut duty.

NASA said both will remain connected to the lunar exploration program as emeritus astronauts. In that role, they will volunteer time to train and mentor agency workers and share lessons from the mission with teams preparing for future flights.

Glover has taken a leadership position at California Polytechnic State University, where he is expected to help shape long-term strategy and encourage students in science and engineering. Wiseman’s next plans were not disclosed; his status change is scheduled to take effect during September.

Artemis II carried Wiseman, Glover, NASA astronaut Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen around the moon, setting a new human distance record. Hansen retired from the Canadian Space Agency in July, leaving Koch as the only crew member still on an active astronaut roster. Wiseman previously spent more than five months aboard the International Space Station and served as NASA’s chief astronaut. Glover flew a nearly six-month SpaceX mission to the station before Artemis II. Their new emeritus roles are intended to preserve that operational experience for NASA’s continuing moon program.
dek: Commander Reid Wiseman and pilot Victor Glover will continue supporting NASA’s lunar program as emeritus astronauts after April’s record-setting moon flight.
headline: Artemis II leaders step away from active astronaut duty

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Los Angeles Rams arrived in Melbourne little more than a day before their season opener against the San Francisco 49ers, testing an unusual travel plan for the NFL’s first regular-season game in Australia.

Friday’s game at the Melbourne Cricket Ground is scheduled for 10:35 a.m. local time. The Rams chose to maintain their normal training rhythm in California and make a late arrival after studying different rest and travel approaches earlier in the year.

San Francisco took the opposite approach, reaching Melbourne more than a week before kickoff to adjust to the time difference. The contrasting schedules turn recovery and body-clock management into a visible part of the matchup.

Los Angeles also considered the return trip. By minimizing its time in Australia, the team hopes to reduce the need for a second major adjustment before a Week Two home game against the New York Giants. The strategy cannot be judged until players face regular-season intensity after the roughly 13,000-kilometer journey. On the field, the Rams enter with high expectations and a familiar offensive group, while their defense has added Myles Garrett and awaits Aaron Donald’s later return from retirement. The opener will provide the first practical test of whether the travel plan preserved performance.
dek: Los Angeles arrived in Melbourne little more than a day before facing San Francisco, relying on months of travel planning to limit jet lag.
headline: Rams test rapid-arrival strategy before NFL’s first regular-season game in Australia

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: NH Chronicle is marking a half-century of mud football in the Mount Washington Valley with a new retrospective on the Hogs, the local team whose name became closely tied to the region’s unusual athletic tradition.

WMUR’s program brings members of the group back together and traces how playing football in mud grew into a recognizable North Conway event. The setting became known as Hog Coliseum, behind the community center in the village.

The story is less about conventional standings than about the people who kept returning to the field and built a durable community identity around the game. The reunion gives former participants a chance to connect the early years with the tradition remembered by later spectators.

For the Mount Washington Valley, the retrospective also preserves a piece of local culture that sits outside the area’s familiar skiing and hiking image. A 50-year run turns what began as a novelty into community history, and WMUR’s account records the people behind it while those memories can still be shared firsthand.
dek: A new WMUR retrospective reunites members of the Hogs and looks back at a muddy football tradition rooted in North Conway.
headline: NH Chronicle revisits 50-year Mud Bowl tradition in Mount Washington Valley

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Forty-eight Manchester students earned New Hampshire’s Seal of Biliteracy in 2026, contributing to the program’s largest statewide cohort since it launched five years ago.

Manchester Ink Link reported that 533 students across New Hampshire received the distinction this year. Because some demonstrated proficiency in more than one additional language, the state issued 547 awards. Languages represented included Spanish, French, Portuguese, Arabic, Ukrainian, Vietnamese, Chinese and American Sign Language, among many others.

The seal recognizes graduating students who meet English requirements and demonstrate intermediate-level proficiency in listening, speaking, reading and writing in another language. Approved assessments include Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate and other state-recognized language tests. Recipients receive a seal on their diploma, a state certificate and a graduation cord.

The Manchester group shows how the recognition is reaching students in the state’s largest school district. State education officials describe multilingual ability as useful for community connections and future work. New Hampshire also recognized 48 middle-school students with a Junior Seal of Biliteracy, extending the program’s pathway to younger learners.
dek: Forty-eight Manchester students earned the state distinction as New Hampshire recognized its largest annual cohort since the program began.
headline: Manchester students help New Hampshire Seal of Biliteracy reach record

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Lindsay Clancy’s defense attorney has asked a Plymouth Superior Court judge to enter a required finding of not guilty after the recent jury deadlock ended her trial in a mistrial.

WHDH reported that attorney Kevin Reddington filed the six-page motion Thursday. The request argues that prosecutors did not present enough evidence for a juror seeking the truth to find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

The filing also challenges whether the state proved that Clancy was mentally capable of conforming her conduct to the law. That issue was central to the case and to the jury’s inability to reach a unanimous verdict. The motion asks Judge William Sullivan to resolve the case rather than send it toward another trial.

A filing is a request, not a ruling, and the court has not yet granted the defense’s motion. The next significant step will be the judge’s response after the prosecution has an opportunity to address the arguments. Until then, the mistrial remains the case’s latest completed proceeding and the criminal charges have not been dismissed.
dek: Attorney Kevin Reddington filed a six-page motion asking the judge to enter a required finding of not guilty after jurors deadlocked.
headline: Lindsay Clancy’s defense seeks not-guilty finding after mistrial

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Fall River police arrested a 21-year-old man Thursday after investigators said a search of a Pulaski Street home uncovered a short-barreled rifle, a suppressor and ammunition.
NBC 10 reported that the department’s Community Action and Suppression Team executed the warrant with assistance from the Emergency Services Unit. Police identified the target as Devin Alves.

Detectives said they recovered a Palmetto State Armory rifle fitted with a 30-round magazine containing 30 live .300 Blackout rounds. Investigators also reported finding a black-powder revolver, 9 mm ammunition and a magazine for a .22-caliber Taurus rifle.

Alves faces charges that include possession of a large-capacity firearm, possession of a firearm and ammunition without the required state credentials, possession of a silencer, possession of a large-capacity feeding device and improper firearm storage. The accusations remain allegations, and the report did not include a court disposition or a response from the defendant. The seizure adds a new case to Fall River’s ongoing enforcement work involving unlawfully held weapons.
dek: Police arrested a 21-year-old after a Pulaski Street search that investigators say recovered multiple weapons and ammunition.
headline: Fall River search finds short-barreled rifle and suppressor, police say

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A 20-year-old Hopkinton resident was airlifted to Rhode Island Hospital after a vehicle crashed into a tree on Route 216 in Ashaway, according to local police.

NBC 10 reported that an officer observed the northbound vehicle traveling at high speed. Police said the officer activated emergency lights in an effort to get the driver to slow down, but the vehicle continued. The officer then traveled in the same direction and found it against a large tree near Trinity Lutheran Church.

The driver was conscious when emergency crews arrived but had significant injuries, police said. Firefighters and medical personnel worked at the scene before the patient was flown to the Providence trauma center.

Hopkinton police said the crash remains under investigation. Officials had not released the driver’s name or described any citation or charge in the report. The inquiry will need to establish the vehicle’s path, speed and other circumstances before investigators can reach conclusions about what caused it to leave the roadway.
dek: Police said a 20-year-old resident suffered serious injuries after a vehicle left the road near Trinity Lutheran Church in Ashaway.
headline: Hopkinton driver airlifted after Route 216 tree crash

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Elaine Pelino filed for a recount Thursday in Rhode Island’s close Republican primary for governor, adding a formal review request to a contest that remained unresolved after election night.

NBC 10 reported that unofficial Board of Elections results showed Aaron Guckian leading Pelino by 279 votes. The posted totals gave Guckian 11,623 votes, or 50.61%, and Pelino 11,344 votes, or 49.4%, based on results updated early Thursday.

State rules required primary recount applications to be submitted by 4 p.m. on the day after the election. The Board of Elections reviews an application to determine whether the contest qualifies. Any recount would take place at the board’s Cranston office and would be open to the public.

Guckian, a trade-association executive, was the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor in 2022 and has the state party’s endorsement. Pelino is a first-time candidate. The eventual winner will advance to the November general election. The posted margin and totals remain unofficial while the recount request is considered.
dek: Unofficial results showed Aaron Guckian ahead by 279 votes as the Board of Elections prepared to review the application.
headline: Elaine Pelino requests recount in Rhode Island governor primary

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Yemen’s Houthi forces have seized the southwestern port city of Mocha after a rapid advance along the Red Sea coast, strengthening their position near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Reuters reported that Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources described direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards during the campaign. Two Iranian sources said Tehran had urged the Houthis to increase attacks on Saudi Arabia and offered additional funding, weapons and senior officers.

Iran publicly rejects descriptions of the Houthis as a proxy. One Iranian official told Reuters that the decision to move on Mocha was the group’s own, while acknowledging that the advance increased pressure on oil markets and on U.S. and Saudi interests.

Control around Bab el-Mandeb matters because the narrow waterway connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and is a major route for shipping and energy cargoes. The reported seizure is a developing military and trade-route risk. Independent access to the battlefield is limited, and claims about command arrangements rely on the sources cited by Reuters.
dek: Sources told Reuters that Iranian guidance and weapons supported a rapid coastal advance that strengthened the group’s position near Bab el-Mandeb.
headline: Houthi seizure of Mocha tightens pressure on Red Sea route

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Iranian strikes damaged several U.S. military aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan this week, according to a U.S. official who spoke to Reuters.

The official said one A-10 Thunderbolt II lost a wing, while roughly eight F-15 aircraft sustained light damage and returned to service. The account did not identify the exact timing of each impact or provide a full estimate of repair costs.

U.S. forces fired about 30 Patriot interceptors to counter incoming missiles during the attack, the official said. The strike followed U.S. attacks on five Iranian crude carriers, which Washington said answered two attempted ballistic-missile attacks on a Navy warship.

The new damage assessment shows that the Jordan strike reached equipment on the base even as defenses responded. It also adds to concerns about aircraft losses and the rate at which air-defense interceptors are being used during the widening conflict. The situation remains developing, and the figures may change as military assessments continue.
dek: A U.S. official told Reuters that an A-10 lost a wing and about eight F-15s sustained light damage during this week’s attack.
headline: Iranian strike damages U.S. aircraft at Jordan base, official says

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Britain has spent nearly $40 million on SpaceX satellite services for military communications, deepening its use of both Starshield and Starlink systems.

The British defense ministry told Reuters it has about 1,000 Starshield terminals and 500 Starlink terminals. It reported spending roughly 13 million pounds on Starshield equipment and airtime and 16.5 million pounds on Starlink.

The disclosure makes Britain the first country outside the United States to publicly acknowledge adopting Starshield, the SpaceX service marketed for military and intelligence missions. Starlink is the company’s better-known consumer and commercial network.

Satellite terminals can provide communications when fixed infrastructure is unavailable, but the purchase also concentrates an important capability with a U.S. private company. European governments have been discussing how to strengthen their own defense technology and reduce dependence on outside systems. Britain’s deployment shows how quickly commercially derived satellite networks have become part of government communications planning, even as questions about resilience, control and long-term supplier dependence remain.
dek: Britain disclosed about 1,000 Starshield and 500 Starlink terminals, making it the first country outside the U.S. to acknowledge Starshield adoption.
headline: UK spends nearly $40 million on SpaceX satellite services

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Iran’s recovery of a U.S. military underwater drone could allow engineers to examine and copy parts of the vessel, creating a technology setback for the Pentagon and manufacturer Anduril.

Reuters identified the vessel as a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle used for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions. The Navy said the older-model drone malfunctioned before Iranian forces recovered it near the Strait of Hormuz.

Analysts cited by Reuters said Iran could study the hardware and reverse-engineer mechanical systems, although the capture is unlikely to produce an immediate, decisive military advantage. The larger value may lie in understanding design choices, materials and how the autonomous craft is assembled.

The episode recalls Iran’s 2011 recovery of an RQ-170 Sentinel reconnaissance drone, after which Tehran displayed aircraft it said drew on the captured system. Autonomous underwater vehicles are designed to operate for extended periods with little human intervention, making reliable recovery and data protection part of their security model. The loss will likely sharpen attention on safeguards for future deployments.
dek: Analysts say the recovered Dive-LD may expose hardware and mechanical systems even if it does not deliver a decisive military advantage.
headline: Captured U.S. underwater drone could give Iran design clues

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: U.S. stocks moved lower Thursday as rising Treasury yields, higher oil prices and August producer-price data increased concern that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates next week.

Reuters reported that the S&P 500, Nasdaq and Dow were each down around six-tenths of a percent during the session. Nvidia and Micron fell, while Apple advanced a day after introducing its folding phone. The figures describe intraday trading and are not live prices.

The 10-year Treasury yield reached its highest level in nearly three years, while the 30-year yield touched a more than 19-year high. Brent crude’s jump to about $107 a barrel added to inflation pressure as disruptions affected major energy routes.

Producer prices rose in line with expectations on a monthly basis, with energy costs rebounding. Futures markets increased the implied chance of a quarter-point Fed increase at the coming meeting. Investors now turn to Friday’s consumer-price report for a broader read on inflation. Higher yields can pressure stock valuations by raising borrowing costs and improving returns available from bonds.
dek: Major U.S. indexes declined Thursday as higher energy costs and producer-price data strengthened expectations for tighter Federal Reserve policy.
headline: Wall Street falls as Treasury yields and inflation fears rise

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The International Monetary Fund said the global economy remains on track to expand about 3% in 2026, although elevated energy prices and debt leave the outlook unusually uncertain.

An IMF spokesperson told Reuters that the economy had absorbed the Middle East war’s energy shock better than initially feared. Countries used reserves, shifted energy sources and reduced demand, but the fund cautioned that the shock is not over and that oil and gas prices remain high.

The IMF’s July estimate was 3.0%, below the average 3.5% growth recorded in 2024 and 2025. The organization plans to issue a revised forecast during its October meetings with the World Bank in Bangkok.

Public debt is approaching 100% of global economic output, the highest level since World War Two, according to the IMF. The fund also said progress in lowering inflation has stalled. For markets, the combination matters because slower growth, persistent inflation and heavy government borrowing can pull interest rates, currencies and asset valuations in different directions.
dek: The fund said the world economy has absorbed the energy shock better than feared, while elevated prices and near-record public debt remain concerns.
headline: IMF sees 3% global growth but warns risks remain high

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, a full generation has grown up without a personal memory of the day, learning about it through relatives, classrooms, online archives and the wars that followed.

Reuters collected accounts from people born around or after 2001 in the United States and other countries. Their experiences show how an event shifts from lived memory to history while continuing to influence ideas about national security, American power and public grief.

For some, the first explanation came from parents who described where they were. Others encountered the attacks through school lessons or images online. The nearly 3,000 deaths remain central to commemoration, but younger people also place the day within a longer story that includes military conflicts and changes in travel and surveillance.

The transition creates a challenge for educators and museums: preserve factual detail and individual experiences without assuming students remember the atmosphere of 2001. The 25th anniversary makes that task more visible as commemorations increasingly bring together witnesses, survivors and adults for whom September 11 has always been a historical event.
dek: Reuters gathered accounts from people too young to remember the attacks about how schools, families and later events shaped their understanding.
headline: A generation understands September 11 as history, not memory

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is preparing a large study of people who were children near the World Trade Center when the towers fell, addressing a major gap in long-term September 11 health research.

Reuters reported that roughly 25,000 children lived or attended school near lower Manhattan in 2001, with thousands more in surrounding neighborhoods. Many encountered dust containing pulverized concrete, glass fibers, asbestos and other pollutants, yet few entered the government-funded studies that largely followed first responders and other adults.

The CDC plans to seek research applications for a World Trade Center Youth Research Coordinating Center and a long-term cohort. Eligible participants would have been 21 or younger, or in utero, and living below 14th Street in Manhattan or anywhere in Brooklyn on and after the attacks. Researchers also plan a similarly aged comparison group without the same exposure.

Key details, including the target number of participants, proposal date and available funding, have not been finalized publicly. Scientists hope the project can clarify possible links to cancers, cardiovascular disease and reproductive outcomes as the exposed population reaches its 30s and early 40s.
dek: The project will seek to identify and track people who were young, infants or in utero near lower Manhattan and Brooklyn after the attacks.
headline: CDC plans major health study of children exposed to 9/11

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Conservationists are monitoring twin light beams projected from the Mount Washington summit for the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, watching for signs that migrating birds are becoming disoriented.

New Hampshire Public Radio reported that the display will continue through the weekend during the peak fall migration period for songbirds. Many songbirds travel at night, and artificial light can attract them or alter their routes. The summit is normally far darker than an urban setting, making the installation’s local effect uncertain.

New Hampshire Audubon has worked with Cornell University scientists, the New York City Bird Alliance, New Hampshire Fish and Game and State Parks on a protocol for switching off the beams if observers see dangerous behavior. During a test earlier in the week, monitors saw birds remain below about 2,000 feet and avoid the new lights.

Observers plan to use binoculars, spotting equipment and a thermal monocular capable of detecting birds and bats. Their weekend watch will help determine whether the memorial can continue safely while migration traffic passes over the White Mountains.
dek: Conservation groups and state agencies have a shutoff protocol as twin memorial beams coincide with peak fall songbird migration.
headline: Bird monitors watch Mount Washington’s September 11 tribute beams

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Hikers planning a White Mountains outing this weekend face sharply different conditions from one day to the next, with slick trails and powerful summit winds Friday followed by a much calmer Saturday.

The Mount Washington Observatory’s recreational forecast said muddy surfaces will linger through Friday. Temperatures at higher elevations may fall below freezing early, while patchy summit fog reduces visibility. A wind chill advisory for the higher summits remains in effect until 10 p.m., and northwest gusts above hurricane force are possible in the morning. Valley and notch gusts could reach 30 mph.

Saturday is expected to bring the best window for longer trips. Sunshine, warmer air and light winds are forecast across elevations. The observatory advised hikers to carry enough water and sun protection despite the cooler start to the weekend.

Sunday should stay warm and mostly dry for much of the day, but moderate west winds and summit fog are expected to return at higher elevations. Clouds will increase, with a chance of showers and isolated thunder Sunday afternoon. A lightweight rain layer remains a sensible addition even for outings that begin under favorable skies.
dek: A rough Friday above treeline is forecast to give way to sunshine, warmer temperatures and lighter winds across New Hampshire’s mountains.
headline: Saturday brings a better White Mountains hiking window

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts’ highest court publicly reprimanded Judge Shelley Joseph on Thursday, closing a disciplinary case that grew out of allegations that a defendant avoided a federal immigration arrest at a Newton courthouse in 2018.

Federal prosecutors charged Joseph in 2019 and dropped the case in 2022 after she agreed to face a state disciplinary review. Prosecutors had alleged that a Dominican man appearing before her was allowed to leave through a rear courthouse door while an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent waited elsewhere in the building.

A disciplinary hearing officer later found that the Judicial Conduct Commission had not proved Joseph knew of a plan to help the defendant evade ICE. The commission ultimately sought a public reprimand rather than suspension or removal.

In a unanimous unsigned opinion, the Supreme Judicial Court found separate violations of judicial conduct rules. It cited an off-the-record discussion with the defendant’s lawyer and Joseph’s suggestion that the man might be held overnight after she learned an ICE officer was present. The court said those actions created an improper appearance even though the alleged knowing role in an escape plan was not established.
dek: The state’s Supreme Judicial Court imposed a public reprimand while emphasizing that investigators did not prove the judge knew of an evasion plan.
headline: Massachusetts high court reprimands judge in ICE courthouse case

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Two 17-year-old boys were arrested after gunfire struck homes in New Bedford’s West End, police said Thursday. No injury to the intended target was reported.

Officers went to the intersection of Chestnut and Willis streets at about 3:30 p.m. Wednesday following reports of shots. They found spent cartridge casings and damage to several nearby houses. Investigators allege that two masked teenagers fired toward a person in the area before leaving the scene.

Police located the teenagers inside a nearby home and recovered two firearms believed to have been used in the shooting. Detectives also seized ammunition, clothing, masks, a 3D printer and a handgun frame that investigators believe was produced with the printer.

Both teenagers face charges that include assault with intent to murder, carrying a loaded firearm without a license and intentionally firing near a building and causing property damage. One also faces allegations tied to manufacturing a firearm with a 3D printer. The accusations remain charges, and the source report did not identify the juveniles.
dek: Police said the intended target was not hurt and investigators recovered two firearms, ammunition and a handgun frame believed to be 3D-printed.
headline: Two teens arrested after gunfire damages New Bedford homes

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Shell’s North American unit has agreed to sell its interests in RISEC Holdings to Constellation Energy for $715 million, transferring ownership of a major Rhode Island power asset if regulators approve the deal.

RISEC owns the Rhode Island State Energy Center, a 609-megawatt, two-unit combined-cycle natural gas plant that supplies the New England power market. The facility is part of the regional generation fleet serving electricity demand across Rhode Island and neighboring states.

Shell also announced a separate transaction to acquire all equity in Hunlock Creek Generating, which owns 169 megawatts of natural gas-fired capacity in Pennsylvania. The company described the paired moves as part of active management of its U.S. power holdings, selling one asset while adding another in a different market.

Both transactions require regulatory approvals and are expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. Until that process is completed, the Rhode Island plant remains under its current ownership structure. The announced price applies to Shell’s RISEC interests, according to Reuters.
dek: Shell’s North American unit agreed to sell RISEC Holdings, owner of a 609-megawatt gas plant serving the New England power market.
headline: Constellation to buy Rhode Island State Energy Center interests for $715 million

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Nine people were displaced after an early-morning fire damaged a multifamily home on Steuben Street in Providence, according to the city fire department.

Firefighters were called to the property at about 2:23 a.m. Thursday. The department said crews located the fire in a bathroom on the third floor. Most of the damage was concentrated on that level, although the lower floors of the building also sustained damage.

The displaced residents include two children. One firefighter was taken to Roger Williams Medical Center with injuries the department described as minor. The report did not identify any injured residents.

Officials had not provided a cause for the fire in the source report. The extent of the lower-floor damage and the timetable for residents to return were also not specified. The incident adds a housing disruption for multiple families while investigators and building officials assess the property. The department’s account did not announce arrests or suggest that the blaze was intentionally set.
dek: A firefighter suffered minor injuries after crews found the blaze in a third-floor bathroom on Steuben Street early Thursday.
headline: Nine displaced in Providence multifamily house fire

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Several people were killed and several others injured Thursday when a travel coach crashed near the Alpine village of Susch in eastern Switzerland, regional police said.

Emergency teams were sent to the crash site in the canton of Graubünden. A spokesperson for the Dutch travel industry association ANVR, speaking for tour operator OAD, said the bus carried 48 passengers and that all were Dutch nationals.

Images published from the scene showed the coach lying on its side with helicopters and emergency vehicles nearby. Authorities had not released an exact death toll, the identities of those killed or details about the severity of the injuries in the initial report.

The cause of the crash was also not immediately reported. Susch is in the Lower Engadine region, where Alpine roads connect communities and mountain passes in southeastern Switzerland. Because casualty figures and investigative details remained incomplete, the situation was still developing Thursday evening. Officials were expected to provide further information after emergency work and passenger notifications.
dek: Police said a travel coach carrying 48 Dutch passengers crashed near Susch in eastern Switzerland, leaving multiple people dead and injured.
headline: Several killed in Swiss Alpine coach crash

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The U.S. Treasury Department announced new sanctions Thursday against companies and individuals it says support Hezbollah and other Iranian-aligned groups, expanding Washington’s economic campaign during the continuing regional conflict.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control targeted people and entities in Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon and Turkey. Treasury said the networks supported Kata’ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi paramilitary group linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps, and Lebanon’s Hezbollah.

The measures fall under Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign Treasury announced August 24 to restrict funding tied to Iran’s military, missile development, cyber activity and the Revolutionary Guard. OFAC also said it would deny most Iran-related license requests except in exceptional circumstances. Separately, a U.S. citizen agreed to pay $1.43 million to resolve potential civil liability involving 39 apparent sanctions violations.

The newest designations did not target Yemen’s Houthis, whose Red Sea advances are creating a separate threat to shipping. The practical effect of the latest sanctions will depend on enforcement and the ability of designated networks to find alternative financial channels.
dek: Treasury targeted entities and individuals in four countries and tightened its approach to Iran-related licensing as the regional conflict continues.
headline: U.S. expands sanctions on networks tied to Iranian proxies

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Financial Services on Thursday, a specialized product aimed initially at investment bankers and equity researchers who work with large volumes of licensed market and company data.

The service combines OpenAI’s latest model with built-in information from providers including LSEG, PitchBook and Daloopa. It also includes material from LSEG News, Crunchbase and Quartr, covering areas such as earnings transcripts, financial statements and company fundamentals. Firms with existing subscriptions can connect additional services through integrations.
