Morgan Stanley and Evercore served as design partners. OpenAI said the product builds on ChatGPT Enterprise security controls, including role-based access and encryption. Compliance teams can export workspace logs into audit processes, an important requirement for firms operating under recordkeeping and supervision rules.

Users can conduct research across multiple sources, build financial models and create client materials using their own templates, according to the company. OpenAI plans to broaden the available data and expand the service beyond investment banking and equity research. The launch reflects growing competition to adapt general-purpose AI systems for regulated, data-intensive industries.
dek: The specialized service combines AI tools with licensed financial datasets and controls designed for regulated firms.
headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT product for financial services

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Positron AI said Thursday that it raised $875 million in a funding round valuing the AI-chip startup at $5 billion, more than four times its valuation seven months earlier.

PitchBook data cited by Reuters showed that Positron raised $230 million in February at a $1.06 billion valuation. The new financing includes a $375 million Series C at a $3.5 billion pre-money valuation and a Series C-1 of as much as $500 million led by NEA and Silicon Graphics founder Jim Clark.

The company plans to use the proceeds to finish the design of Asimov, its next-generation processor, with production targeted for the second half of 2027. Positron focuses on inference, the stage in which trained AI models respond to user requests, a market where specialized chips are challenging Nvidia’s position.

Positron said its planned Titan system will combine four to eight Asimov chips in one node for very large models and long context windows. It is also deploying more than 50 racks of its first-generation Atlas inference system at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, according to the company.
dek: The startup said the round values it at $5 billion and will fund final design work on its Asimov processor.
headline: Positron raises $875 million for next-generation AI inference chip

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The global AI investment boom has become large enough to influence economic conditions and deserves closer financial-stability scrutiny, Bank for International Settlements chief Pablo Hernández de Cos said Thursday.

The BIS estimates that the five largest technology companies will invest more than $1 trillion in AI across 2025 and 2026. Industry projections cited by the central-bank organization put global AI investment at about $500 billion now and as much as $4 trillion by 2030.

Hernández de Cos said high valuations, concentrated markets and less transparent financing could create vulnerabilities if corporate profits fail to meet expectations. A growing share of AI infrastructure spending is being financed with debt and private credit instead of current earnings, increasing links between technology investment and financial markets.

The warning was not a forecast of a crash. The BIS chief also cited studies finding productivity gains of 10% to 65% in particular tasks, including coding and professional writing. For investors and policymakers, the central issue is whether those task-level gains spread across the economy quickly enough to justify the scale and financing cost of current spending.
dek: Pablo Hernández de Cos pointed to concentrated valuations and increasingly opaque debt financing while acknowledging AI’s productivity potential.
headline: BIS chief warns AI investment boom is creating financial-stability risks

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Interest-rate futures shifted toward a Federal Reserve increase next week after new data showed U.S. producer prices rose 5.4% in the 12 months through August.

Reuters reported that traders placed the probability of a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s September 15–16 meeting near 70%, up from roughly 65% before Thursday’s reports. The central bank has held its policy rate in a 3.50% to 3.75% range since December.

The overall wholesale-price increase matched economists’ expectations, but details suggested inflation pressure may be broadening. Transportation and warehousing costs rose, along with hospital-service prices and airfares. Reuters also noted that disrupted oil distribution from the Middle East conflict and heavy electronics demand linked to AI investment are adding pressure.

Friday’s consumer-price report is likely to shape the final market view before the meeting. Futures probabilities are not a guarantee of Federal Reserve action and can change quickly as new data arrive. Investors are watching whether inflation remains too persistent for policymakers to keep rates unchanged while the labor market appears stable.
dek: Futures markets put the chance of a quarter-point move near 70% after August wholesale inflation, with consumer prices still due Friday.
headline: Traders raise odds of September Fed rate increase after producer-price data

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New England Patriots receiver A.J. Brown will undergo additional evaluation after injuring an ankle in the season opener, leaving his availability for Week 2 uncertain.

Coach Mike Vrabel said Thursday that the team needed more test results before deciding whether Brown could play in New England’s next game. Brown was hurt early in the third quarter of the Patriots’ 13-10 loss at Seattle on Wednesday and did not return.

Brown finished the opener with three receptions for 26 yards. His exit reduced the options available to quarterback Drake Maye as Seattle erased New England’s early lead and completed its fourth-quarter comeback. The Patriots’ offense will now prepare with multiple contingencies while Brown’s recovery is assessed.

New England is scheduled to host Pittsburgh on September 20. The longer-than-usual gap following the Wednesday opener gives Brown additional treatment and recovery time, but the team had not announced a firm practice or game status in the source report. Injury designations later in the preparation week should provide a clearer indication of whether he can return.
dek: Patriots coach Mike Vrabel said the receiver needs additional testing after leaving New England’s season-opening loss in Seattle.
headline: A.J. Brown’s Week 2 status uncertain after ankle injury

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The British Museum opened its sold-out Bayeux Tapestry exhibition to the public Thursday, giving visitors in London a close view of the nearly 1,000-year-old embroidery.

The work has left France for the first time since the 11th century and is scheduled to remain at the museum for 10 months. Its stitched scenes depict the Norman invasion of England in 1066 and the events surrounding the Battle of Hastings, making it one of Europe’s best-known visual historical records.

The 70-meter tapestry is displayed in a purpose-built glass case. Ticket holders receive 40 minutes on an elevated platform before moving closer to examine the stitching. The museum’s arrangement is designed to show both the full narrative sequence and small details that are difficult to appreciate in reproductions.

Demand exhausted the available tickets before the public opening, and the exhibition has generated widespread attention across Britain. The loan is unusual because of the tapestry’s age, fragility and national significance in France. Its extended London stay gives scholars and museum visitors a rare chance to study the object outside its longtime home in Bayeux.
dek: The nearly 1,000-year-old embroidery left France for the first time since the 11th century and will remain at the British Museum for 10 months.
headline: Bayeux Tapestry opens sold-out London exhibition

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The U.S. Justice Department has directed New Hampshire to preserve paper ballots and electronic records from the 2024 election beyond the state’s normal retention period, according to a letter reported by New Hampshire Public Radio.

The September 4 letter instructed Secretary of State David Scanlan to retain all hard-copy ballots, citing ongoing litigation without identifying a case. New Hampshire municipalities ordinarily may destroy paper ballots 22 months after an election. Similar federal instructions have reportedly gone to at least 30 states.

Scanlan subsequently told local election officials to preserve all 2024 ballots and related records. He said the federal government had supplied no factual or legal basis for the demand and emphasized that the ballots remain confidential. Any future request to inspect or copy them would be evaluated individually, he said.

The federal letter also sought preservation of electronic election records and referred to potential Civil Rights Act violations without presenting evidence. State officials said they had no basis to believe New Hampshire violated election law. The request arrives just after the state primary, which officials said proceeded without significant problems.
dek: The state says the request cites unspecified litigation and provides no factual or legal basis for suggesting New Hampshire violated election law.
headline: Federal Justice Department tells New Hampshire to retain 2024 ballots

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New Hampshire’s state primary concluded without significant incidents, according to the state Department of Justice, after election-law personnel monitored voting across hundreds of polling places.

The department said 39 inspectors from its Election Law Unit visited about 260 polling locations. Their work included observing procedures and assisting local officials when questions arose. The department coordinated with the Secretary of State’s office during the voting period.

A dedicated hotline staffed by four attorneys, two investigators and a paralegal received 83 contacts. The state did not identify any of those calls as producing a significant election problem. Secretary of State David Scanlan said he had no concerns about disruption and noted that state personnel routinely monitor elections and help local administrators.

Federal election monitors were also assigned to Manchester and Nashua. New Hampshire was one of six states receiving federal monitors for the primary. The state’s report provides an initial operational assessment rather than a certification of every result; official canvassing and other post-election procedures continue under the normal schedule.
dek: State inspectors visited roughly 260 polling places, while an election-law hotline handled 83 contacts without a significant incident.
headline: New Hampshire election monitors report smooth state primary

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A second suspect has been charged with murder in the Taunton shooting that killed one person and injured seven others at a large house party, prosecutors said Thursday.

Malkiah Cunningham, 25, of New Bedford faces one murder count and seven counts of armed assault with intent to murder. Sienna Barboza, 25, had previously been charged with the same offenses. The charges are allegations, and both defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Police were called to 261 Weir Street at about 12:37 a.m. Sunday after gunfire erupted at a gathering that prosecutors said drew as many as 60 people. The victims were adults in their 20s. Zirovick Depina, 22, of Brockton, died from his injuries.

Prosecutors allege that Barboza drove an SUV to the scene and that Cunningham and another person, who had not been publicly identified in the source report, got out and fired toward the party. The investigation remains active as authorities work to identify all participants and establish the sequence of events.
dek: Prosecutors charged a New Bedford man in the shooting that killed 22-year-old Zirovick Depina and wounded seven other people.
headline: Second suspect charged with murder in Taunton party shooting

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Fall River man has been sentenced to time served after admitting that he mailed cocaine from California to Massachusetts, federal prosecutors said Thursday.

Justin Dupras, 44, received a sentence of two days already served in U.S. District Court in Boston. He pleaded guilty in May 2025 to attempted possession of cocaine with intent to distribute. The sentence resolves the federal criminal charge described in the government’s case.

Prosecutors said Dupras mailed approximately two kilograms of cocaine from Los Angeles to Fall River on December 17, 2024, returned to Massachusetts and collected the package two days later. Investigators also linked him to earlier shipments of more than two kilograms from Chino Hills in September 2024 and about two kilograms from Los Angeles the following month.

Flight records showed same-day return trips connected to the shipments, according to prosecutors. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service investigated with Fall River police. The announced sentence concerns Dupras’s attempt to receive the December package and does not alter the government’s description of the earlier suspected shipments.
dek: Federal prosecutors said the defendant shipped kilogram quantities from California before collecting a package in Fall River.
headline: Fall River man sentenced in California cocaine-mailing case

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Two people were taken to a hospital after a tree fell across Church Avenue and struck an occupied vehicle in Warwick on Thursday afternoon, police said.

Emergency crews received the report at about 3:22 p.m. Firefighters helped all three people inside the vehicle get out safely. Two occupants were transported with injuries described as not life-threatening, while the third person did not require the same reported level of treatment.

Authorities did not immediately identify the occupants or provide a detailed description of the vehicle’s damage. The source report also did not specify what caused the tree to fall, whether weather or the tree’s condition played a role, or how long the road was affected.

Police said the incident remained under investigation. The limited initial account establishes that the vehicle was occupied when the tree came down and that emergency personnel were able to reach everyone inside. Additional findings, including any traffic impacts or property assessment, had not been announced in the report.
dek: Firefighters helped three occupants out of the vehicle after a tree came down across Church Avenue Thursday afternoon.
headline: Two hospitalized after tree falls on vehicle in Warwick

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Providence City Council member Carmen Castillo has requested a recount in the Ward 9 Democratic primary after unofficial results showed a two-vote margin.

The Rhode Island Board of Elections’ preliminary count listed Juan Pichardo with 625 votes, or 50.08%, and Castillo with 623 votes, or 49.92%. The figures are unofficial and may be reviewed through the recount and certification process.

Castillo filed her application before the 4 p.m. deadline on the day after the primary, according to the report. The Board of Elections will determine whether the request qualifies under state recount rules and, if so, how the review will proceed.

The filing does not change the current unofficial totals or declare a winner. It begins an administrative process designed to examine ballots and tabulation in a contest separated by only two votes. Ward 9 voters and both campaigns will need to wait for the board’s decision and the completion of any authorized recount before the result is final.
dek: Unofficial results put Juan Pichardo ahead by two votes in the Democratic contest for the City Council seat.
headline: Carmen Castillo seeks recount in Providence Ward 9 primary

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Israel said Thursday that its military had destroyed an underground Hezbollah complex at the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, marking a new development in the conflict along the border.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz said the operation completed the consolidation of what Israel describes as a security zone. They said Israeli forces would remain in the area to prevent Hezbollah from rebuilding positions. The ridge is roughly 15 kilometers, or 10 miles, from the Israeli border.

The Israeli military said the underground network extended more than two kilometers and contained rockets, missiles, drones, anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives. It also described the site as a command complex for Hezbollah’s Badr unit. Those battlefield claims were made by Israel and were not independently verified in the source report.

Lebanon’s state news agency reported a powerful blast that was felt around Nabatieh. The destruction and Israel’s statement that its troops will stay in the area underscore the continuing risk of escalation and leave questions about the duration and legal status of the military presence.
dek: Israeli leaders said forces demolished a tunnel network at the Ali al-Taher ridge, about 15 kilometers from the border.
headline: Israel says it destroyed Hezbollah underground complex in Lebanon

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Algeria severed diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, an abrupt rupture between two Arab governments whose ties had been strained for years.

The Algerian government cited what it called provocative and hostile actions but did not specify the conduct behind the decision. It said efforts to preserve the relationship had been exhausted. Algerian media have previously accused the UAE of trying to sow discord, adding to an increasingly public dispute.

The UAE responded that it hoped the break would be temporary and said it remained committed to relations based on shared interests. The statement left open the possibility of future diplomatic engagement but did not announce a mediation effort or timeline.

Ending formal relations can affect ambassadorial representation and routine government coordination, though neither side immediately detailed the practical measures that would follow. The lack of a specific allegation from Algiers also leaves the immediate trigger unclear. Further statements will determine whether the decision expands into broader restrictions or remains a diplomatic protest.
dek: Algiers cited unspecified hostile actions, while the UAE said it hoped the rupture would be temporary.
headline: Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with United Arab Emirates

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Anthropic said Thursday that it disrupted several malicious campaigns involving its Claude models, including suspected Russian cyberespionage and efforts by China-based AI companies to extract or replicate the system’s capabilities.

The company said the activity unfolded over eight months and increasingly used multiple AI agents to divide and automate tasks. Anthropic alleged that seven China-based laboratories, including Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek and Xiaomi, accessed Claude through deceptive accounts or intermediaries.

One operation attributed to Alibaba generated 151 million exchanges from May through July and peaked at about 3 million in a day across more than 3,500 allegedly fraudulent accounts, Anthropic said. It also accused Moonshot and DeepSeek of routing some live customer conversations through Claude for training, including potentially sensitive material.

Anthropic separately said tradecraft consistent with the Russia-linked group known as Midnight Blizzard used AI in phishing, hotel Wi-Fi compromise and WhatsApp account takeover attempts targeting Ukrainian officials. The organizations named in the report did not all provide immediate responses. The findings are Anthropic’s account of its own enforcement work and should be read as company allegations, not independent legal determinations.
dek: The company described alleged cyberespionage and large-scale attempts to extract Claude’s capabilities over an eight-month period.
headline: Anthropic says it disrupted Russian and Chinese AI-abuse campaigns

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Oracle reported quarterly results above Wall Street estimates Thursday as demand for artificial-intelligence computing added more than $30 billion in new cloud contracts.

The company’s remaining performance obligations, a measure of contracted future revenue, reached $664 billion. That exceeded the $639.89 billion estimate compiled by Visible Alpha. Oracle said it expects roughly half of the backlog to convert into sales within 36 months.

Heavy data-center investment remains central to the outlook. Oracle projected annual spending of $90 billion to $95 billion, while noting that many customers prepay or bring their own hardware. Free cash flow was negative $5.40 billion, a smaller outflow than the negative $9.56 billion analysts had expected.

Oracle forecast adjusted fiscal 2027 earnings of $8.10 per share, slightly above the $8.05 consensus cited by Reuters. Reuters reported that the shares rose about 4% in extended trading after having fallen more than 21% during the year. The results eased some concerns about cash burn, but the large spending plan still makes the pace of contract conversion a key test.
dek: The company reported more than $30 billion in new AI-cloud contracts and a smaller-than-expected free-cash-flow outflow.
headline: Oracle beats estimates as AI cloud contracts expand backlog

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Chip designer Altera is preparing a U.S. initial public offering that could raise more than $2 billion, people familiar with the plans told Reuters.

The Silver Lake- and Intel-backed company has selected Barclays, Citigroup, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley as underwriters, according to the report. A confidential filing could come within weeks, and a listing may follow this year. The timing, size and bank assignments are not final and could change.

If completed at the reported scale, the offering would be the largest semiconductor IPO since Arm raised about $5 billion in 2023. Altera makes programmable chips used across communications, industrial and data-center applications, placing the transaction within an active market for computing infrastructure.

The broader U.S. IPO market has already produced a record $137 billion in proceeds through August when special-purpose acquisition companies are excluded, according to Dealogic data cited by Reuters. Altera’s filing would test whether investor demand can support another large chip offering. No final valuation or offer price was reported, and the company has not yet completed a public listing.
dek: Sources told Reuters the chip designer could seek more than $2 billion in a listing, though timing and size may still change.
headline: Silver Lake and Intel-backed Altera prepares large U.S. IPO

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The average U.S. diesel price moved above $6 a gallon Thursday for the first time, according to fuel-tracking service GasBuddy, intensifying pressure on freight operators and supply chains.

GasBuddy said the national average was roughly $2.30 higher than a year earlier. The increase has followed supply disruptions tied to the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, both of which have tightened availability of the middle distillates used in trucking and industrial activity.

U.S. diesel inventories stood at 106.3 million barrels, about 13% below the five-year average, Energy Information Administration data showed. Crude prices also remained elevated Thursday: Brent settled at $107.63 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate at $102.48, Reuters reported.

Diesel costs matter beyond the pump because they feed into shipping, agriculture and construction expenses. The reported national average is a broad benchmark and local prices can differ substantially by taxes and supply conditions. With inventories below normal, businesses and inflation watchers will be focused on whether refinery output and international flows can rebuild stocks.
dek: Tight inventories and disruptions linked to the Iran war and attacks on Russian refineries have pushed freight fuel costs sharply higher.
headline: U.S. average diesel price crosses $6, GasBuddy reports

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Tommy Hilfiger returned to New York Fashion Week on Thursday with a spring and summer 2027 show staged in the lobby of Manhattan’s Plaza Hotel.

Model Gigi Hadid opened the presentation, which featured oversized polo shirts, plaid bucket hats and a palette built around red, navy and other bold colors. Guests watched from green armchairs arranged through the hotel lobby, turning the landmark interior into part of the collection’s visual setting.

The location carried a personal connection for Hilfiger, who lived in a Plaza penthouse for more than a decade. Now 75, the designer founded his namesake brand in 1985 and said the label is continuing to pursue younger shoppers, including Generation Z. The company is owned by PVH.

Attendees included Kate Moss, Camila Cabello, Jisoo, New York Knicks players Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart, and actor Patrick Schwarzenegger. The event took place on the first official day of the fashion-week calendar and used a familiar New York institution to frame Hilfiger’s latest take on American sportswear.
dek: The designer presented his spring and summer 2027 collection inside the Manhattan hotel, with Gigi Hadid opening the show.
headline: Tommy Hilfiger returns to New York Fashion Week at the Plaza

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Jean Smart and Harrison Ford enter Monday’s Emmy Awards with the chance to reach distinct career milestones as the television industry gathers in Los Angeles.

Smart could become the first performer to win best comedy actress in every season of a show’s run if she earns a fifth award for Hacks. Ford, 84, is nominated for Shrinking and is seeking the first Emmy of his career despite decades of film and television work.

The Pitt is favored in the best-drama race for a second consecutive year, and its star Noah Wyle is also contending for a second straight acting award. Mariska Hargitay will host the ceremony, scheduled for 8 p.m. Eastern on NBC and Peacock. Michael J. Fox is set to receive a humanitarian honor.

The celebration arrives while Hollywood faces production cutbacks, consolidation and anxiety over artificial intelligence. Paramount Skydance’s proposed Warner Bros. Discovery deal is among the business shifts hanging over the industry. The awards will recognize the past television season even as studios, workers and audiences navigate a rapidly changing market.
dek: Smart could complete a five-season awards sweep for Hacks, while Ford is seeking the first Emmy of his career for Shrinking.
headline: Jean Smart and Harrison Ford approach Emmy milestones

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Chester’s Planning Board has continued a public hearing on the proposed Village at Buxton Farm until September 30, giving the town’s engineering consultant more time to complete an environmental review and evaluate the latest project plans.

The proposal calls for 34 detached one- and two-bedroom rental homes at 611 Haverhill Road under Chester’s fair-market housing ordinance. Developer David Haddad requested the delay because the consultant’s reports were not ready for the board’s September 9 meeting.

Testing found PFAS in soil at the former farm field, where biosolids had previously been spread, but did not detect the chemicals in groundwater. An Edgewater Environmental Services report said the finding does not automatically prevent development. It recommended keeping affected soil on the property, minimizing disturbance, stabilizing or capping exposed areas and using erosion controls.

The homes would share one well. The developer said groundwater monitoring would continue and that the project would follow any additional environmental requirements. The next hearing is expected to give the board and residents a fuller record on both the PFAS management plan and Chester’s review of the housing proposal.
dek: The Planning Board moved its review of a proposed 34-home rental community to September 30 while engineers finish environmental and plan reviews.
headline: Chester delays Buxton Farm housing hearing for PFAS review

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Springworks Farm lettuce has disappeared from Hannaford shelves in New Hampshire and across the supermarket chain’s regional footprint, while the status of the Lisbon, Maine, aquaponics business remains unclear.

Manchester Ink Link reported that Springworks stopped supplying Hannaford and other customers weeks ago. The farm’s phone was disconnected, employees did not respond to outreach and its website no longer displayed a store-locator page. Hannaford had not provided a public explanation before the outlet’s deadline.

Springworks had been Hannaford’s exclusive supplier of organic romaine for all 184 stores in New England and New York. Founded in 2014 by Trevor Kenkel, the company used aquaponics, combining greenhouse crops with recirculating water from fish production. By 2024, its products reportedly reached about 300 stores and institutions, including Whole Foods, Roche Bros., Food City, Sysco Northern New England and Maine schools.

The company announced $22 million in financing in 2023 for a new greenhouse, but the current status of that expansion was not established in the report. The available evidence shows a halt in retail supply, not a confirmed permanent closure.
dek: The Maine aquaponics grower that supplied organic romaine across Hannaford’s footprint has stopped appearing on store shelves, with its business status unresolved.
headline: Springworks lettuce disappears from Hannaford as farm status remains unclear

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Singer and television host Jennifer Hudson visited the Charlestown Boys & Girls Club during a recent Boston stop, meeting members and offering encouragement to young people interested in performing.

Hudson answered questions from students and spoke about continuing to pursue a goal even when fear is present. The visit had a personal connection: she took part in a Boys & Girls Club program while growing up in Chicago and told the Charlestown group that the experience helped shape her own path.

Club members also created a version of the “Spirit Tunnel,” the welcoming routine associated with Hudson’s daytime show. The appearance gave aspiring musicians and performers a chance to hear directly from an artist whose career has included music, film, theater and television.

Hudson was in the area promoting the fifth season of “The Jennifer Hudson Show,” which is scheduled to premiere Monday and air locally on WHDH. For the club, the visit paired a celebrity appearance with a practical message about persistence, confidence and making use of community programs that give young people room to develop their interests.
dek: The singer and talk-show host met Boys & Girls Club members, answered questions and shared advice with young people interested in music.
headline: Jennifer Hudson encourages young performers at Charlestown club

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Massachusetts State Police trooper accused of punching another off-duty trooper at a Quincy bar appeared in court Thursday, but his arraignment on an assault-and-battery charge was deferred until October 10.

Christopher Regan, 40, is accused of striking the other trooper at The Reel House in June. According to the source report, surveillance video from the bar captured the alleged punch. The other trooper declined to provide investigators with details about the encounter or information about hospital treatment.

State Police said Regan has been relieved of duty while the department prepares a formal hearing on his employment status. The administrative process is separate from the criminal case, which remains pending.

The charge is an allegation, and Regan is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. The delayed arraignment means the court has not yet taken the next formal step on the accusation. Additional details about what preceded the encounter, any defense response and the department’s duty-status decision had not been announced in the report.
dek: Christopher Regan is accused of punching another off-duty trooper at a Quincy bar; the charge remains an allegation and the case has not been decided.
headline: Massachusetts trooper’s Quincy assault arraignment deferred to October

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Students at Cranston High School West planted 2,977 American flags outside Alumni Auditorium on Thursday, creating a memorial for every person killed in the September 11, 2001, attacks.

The school’s Young Americans for Freedom chapter organized the display as part of the national “Never Forget” project. Students and teachers said the field of flags gives a human scale to an event that happened before today’s high-school students were born.

The installation comes as communities mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks. For students learning about September 11 as history rather than lived memory, the project turns the casualty count into a visible tribute spread across the school grounds.

The flags are scheduled to remain in place through September 12. Organizers described the display as both a remembrance and an invitation for students to ask questions about the victims, first responders and the long-term effects of the attacks. Cranston West’s project is one of many local observances planned across New England for the anniversary.
dek: The memorial outside Alumni Auditorium marks 25 years since the attacks and gives each person killed a visible place in the school display.
headline: Cranston West students plant 2,977 flags for September 11 victims

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Volunteers with the Manville Share Shack are collecting and sorting back-to-school clothing for Rhode Island children whose families need help starting the academic year.

Founders Annette and Tom Briand organized the effort with Pretty Cares Inc., a Woonsocket nonprofit. The Enrico Caruso Club in Lincoln donated space on Labor Day so volunteers could bring the collection together, assess donations and prepare items for distribution.

The organizers used social media to connect with both donors and families. The request focused on practical school clothing, turning individual contributions into a coordinated community supply rather than a conventional resale operation.

The clothing is expected to be distributed at a free community event next weekend. Organizers had not published a final count of donated items or participating families in the source report, but the sorting effort was already underway. The drive extends the Share Shack’s neighborhood model: residents leave usable goods and others take what they need, with no charge and a focus on keeping support local.
dek: The Manville Share Shack and Pretty Cares are sorting donated clothing for a free community distribution planned for next weekend.
headline: Manville volunteers prepare back-to-school clothes for local children

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Two people were killed and seven were injured in drone attacks across Russia’s Belgorod region, regional authorities said Thursday, in the latest reported violence along the border with Ukraine.

Officials said one man died when a drone detonated at an unspecified facility in Novy Oskol. Five people were reported injured in attacks across several other localities. In Shebekino, another man was killed when a drone struck a car, while a woman traveling in the vehicle was injured.

Belgorod has been repeatedly targeted during the war because of its proximity to the Ukrainian border. The initial report did not provide a complete account of property damage, identify all of the injured or establish whether military sites were among the targets.

The casualty figures and circumstances were reported by Russian regional authorities and could not be independently verified in the immediate account. Responsibility was attributed to Ukrainian drones by those officials. The situation remains developing, and later reports may revise the number of casualties or add details about the locations struck.
dek: Regional authorities reported fatalities in Novy Oskol and Shebekino as attacks continued across Russia’s border region.
headline: Two killed, seven injured in Belgorod drone attacks, officials say

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A federal appeals court in Boston declined Thursday to let the U.S. Postal Service implement new mail-ballot requirements while litigation continues, leaving a lower-court injunction in place ahead of the November election.

The rule would require states to provide lists of mail-ballot recipients and place unique barcodes on ballot envelopes. The Postal Service could refuse ballots that did not meet the requirements. A three-judge First Circuit panel said election regulation belongs primarily to states and Congress and cited the risk that voters could be disenfranchised if ballots were rejected.

The Justice Department argued that the requirements were modest mail-processing regulations and asked the court to pause the injunction. The Postal Service has said it acted lawfully. States challenging the rule contend that the executive branch lacks authority to impose the conditions and that election systems cannot be reworked safely so close to voting.

The administration has separately asked the Supreme Court to lift the injunction. Thursday’s ruling does not resolve the underlying lawsuit; it determines which rules apply while the case proceeds. All 50 states permit mail voting in at least some circumstances.
dek: The Boston-based appeals court declined to pause an injunction against federal requirements involving voter lists and ballot barcodes before the November election.
headline: First Circuit keeps block on new USPS mail-ballot rule

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Pentagon is discussing a loan of about $5 billion to AI cloud startup Fluidstack, the Wall Street Journal reported Thursday, as the United States looks to expand the domestic supply chain behind data centers.

Reuters said the potential financing would come from the Defense Department’s Office of Strategic Capital. The money would support manufacturing capacity for selected data-center components rather than directly fund construction of a new AI facility, according to the report.
Neither the Defense Department nor Fluidstack immediately commented to Reuters. The talks therefore do not represent a completed loan, and the final amount or terms could change.

The proposal follows a national-emergency order issued last month that restricted some foreign equipment used by the U.S. power grid. The Office of Strategic Capital has also backed companies in areas such as rare-earth materials and drones. A Fluidstack loan would extend that industrial-policy approach to the computing and electrical hardware needed for large AI systems, where shortages or foreign dependence could slow data-center deployment.
dek: The proposed financing would support domestic production of data-center components as Washington treats AI infrastructure as a strategic supply-chain priority.
headline: Pentagon discusses $5 billion Fluidstack loan, WSJ reports

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Adobe reported third-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates Thursday and said annual recurring revenue from products built around generative AI more than doubled from a year earlier.

Revenue totaled $6.76 billion, compared with an average analyst estimate of $6.70 billion compiled by LSEG. Adjusted profit was $6.13 per share, also ahead of the $6.09 estimate. The results indicate that AI features are beginning to contribute more meaningfully to Adobe’s subscription business.

For the fourth quarter, the company forecast revenue of $6.80 billion to $6.85 billion. The midpoint, $6.825 billion, was slightly below the $6.85 billion analyst estimate. Reuters reported that Adobe shares fell 1.9% in extended trading; that move was a reported after-hours figure, not a live quote.

Adobe also said Anil Chakravarthy will become chief executive on December 1, while longtime leader Shantanu Narayen will move to executive chair. The transition arrives as the company tries to turn AI tools into durable growth while facing competition from a new generation of design and content-creation services.
dek: Quarterly sales and adjusted profit topped expectations, while the midpoint of Adobe’s next-quarter revenue forecast came in slightly below analysts’ estimate.
headline: Adobe revenue beats estimates as AI-first recurring sales double

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: American Eagle Outfitters shares fell sharply Thursday after the apparel retailer forecast flat gross margins for the current quarter and described continued weakness at its namesake brand.

The company kept its annual comparable-sales forecast unchanged after reporting second-quarter revenue above analysts’ expectations. Reuters said uneven discretionary spending and excess inventory have forced heavier promotions, particularly in women’s denim, putting pressure on profitability even as the Aerie intimates and activewear business remained stronger.

American Eagle has increased its investment in denim marketing to reach younger shoppers, but the core label continues to lose ground to competitors. Inventory costs were 14% higher from a year earlier, reflecting tariffs and other expenses, according to the report.

The share decline cited by Reuters occurred during Thursday’s trading and should not be read as a live price. The market reaction highlights investors’ concern that revenue resilience may not translate into stronger earnings while clearance activity remains elevated. American Eagle’s next results will show whether inventory reductions and new product campaigns can stabilize the flagship brand.
dek: The retailer kept its annual comparable-sales forecast after a revenue beat, but discounting and excess inventory continued to weigh on expectations.
headline: American Eagle shares slide on flat margin outlook and core-brand weakness

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Japan’s wholesale prices rose 7.6% in August from a year earlier, keeping pipeline inflation elevated before the Bank of Japan’s policy meeting next week.

The increase in the corporate goods price index was slightly above the 7.4% rise economists had forecast in a Reuters poll. July’s gain was revised to 7.7%. On a month-to-month basis, producer prices slipped 0.2% after a revised 0.4% increase in July.
The yen-based import price index climbed 24.8% from a year earlier, slowing from a revised 29.3% increase in July but still signaling substantial pressure from imported goods and currency moves.

Markets had nearly fully priced a Bank of Japan rate increase to 1.25% from 1%, Reuters reported. A separate poll expected the central bank to reach 1.25% next week and 1.75% in the second quarter of 2027. Those expectations are market forecasts, not announced decisions. The BOJ raised its policy rate to a 31-year high of 1% in June and left it unchanged in July.
dek: Producer prices stayed above forecasts in August, reinforcing expectations that the central bank could raise its policy rate next week.
headline: Japan wholesale inflation holds at 7.6% before Bank of Japan meeting

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Runners left Boston carrying two American flags on a 228-mile relay to Ground Zero, marking 25 years since the September 11 attacks and honoring the people killed.

The flags represent the two hijacked planes that departed Logan International Airport. Relay for America organized the route as a symbolic effort to retrace and reclaim the path from Boston to New York through remembrance and public service.

Each relay segment is 9.11 miles. Boston police escorted the first leg, and organizers said police or fire escorts were confirmed for 20 portions of the journey. First responders are also joining runners along the route.

The nonstop relay is designed to connect communities between the two cities while keeping the victims’ names and the role of emergency personnel in public view. Its arrival at Ground Zero will coincide with anniversary observances in New York. Organizers framed the run not as a race but as a moving memorial carried from the airport where the flights began to the site where many of the victims died.
dek: Relay for America runners are carrying two flags along the route associated with the planes that departed Logan Airport on September 11, 2001.
headline: Flag relay begins 228-mile journey from Boston to Ground Zero
location: Boston, MA to New York, NY

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: FIFA President Gianni Infantino appears to have enough support to win reelection next year, prompting opponents to shift their attention toward reducing presidential power and strengthening governance controls, according to Reuters interviews with people familiar with the discussions.

Infantino faced the most serious challenge of his decade in office after a proposal to sell a 20% stake in FIFA competitions collapsed in July. UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF opposed the plan, while several European national federations withdrew their support.

Reuters reported that Infantino retains strong relationships with many smaller national associations and support across Oceania, Africa and South America. No viable challenger has emerged before the November 18 nomination deadline, and potential candidates cited in football circles have declined to run.

Opponents are therefore considering a campaign for structural changes, including greater transparency and stronger checks on major commercial decisions. Infantino is seeking another term in the March 18, 2027, election in Rabat. The assessment of his support is based on Reuters sourcing rather than a completed vote; national associations will make the formal decision at the election.
dek: Reuters sources say the FIFA president retains enough association support to survive the challenge, pushing critics to focus on checks on executive power.
headline: Infantino opponents shift toward FIFA governance reform as challenge falters

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Epsom Village Water District is operating with one commissioner and no clerk, secretary or treasurer, a staffing crisis that is delaying a planned PFAS treatment project and raising questions about the district’s future.

Commissioner Donna Dudley is the only remaining member of the board after a second commissioner resigned in August. The district serves about 320 connections and roughly 800 people, including Epsom Central School, the town hall, library, fire department and other public buildings. Its system also supplies water to local fire hydrants.

The vacancies make it difficult to assemble a quorum, approve engineering work and move the PFAS project to bidding. Residents are also confronting higher operating costs: the town’s annual hydrant rental charge rose from $9,000 to $40,000, according to the Concord Monitor.

A public meeting is scheduled for September 21 at 6 p.m. at Epsom Central School with town selectmen, state environmental officials and residents. One option under discussion is dissolving the village district and transferring the system to the town, a change that would require voter approval. Until governance is stabilized, the treatment project and other decisions remain constrained.
dek: A one-member board and vacant administrative posts are delaying bids for a treatment project while the district weighs whether the town should assume control.
headline: Epsom water district staffing crisis stalls PFAS remediation

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Kearsarge Regional School Board has set a long-term goal of operating two elementary schools, recommending the eventual closure of Simonds Elementary in Warner and Sutton Central in Bradford.

Superintendent Michael Bessette told families that the target would be implemented in summer 2028 and would not affect the 2026-27 school year. A final closure cannot be made by the board alone: voters in the affected communities would have to approve the plan. A citizen petition could bring the issue to a vote sooner.

District leaders cited major repair needs, taxpayer costs and the challenge of maintaining very small classes across several buildings. Consolidation could concentrate students and staff while limiting future capital spending, but the proposal has drawn concern from parents and residents who said they learned of the recommendation with little warning.

The board’s action establishes a planning direction, not an immediate shutdown order. Enrollment, transportation, staffing, building conditions and the use of any closed properties will require further public review. Families should expect additional meetings and formal votes before the district can move from recommendation to implementation.
dek: The regional school board recommends closing Simonds Elementary and Sutton Central as part of a long-term consolidation plan, with local votes still required.
headline: Kearsarge board targets two-school elementary model by summer 2028

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Capron Park Zoo in Attleboro is mourning longtime zookeeper Kayla St. George, who died at age 39 following a stroke.

St. George had worked at Capron Park for about five years. Her path in animal care included studies at the University of Rhode Island, internships at Mystic Aquarium and Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium, and positions at Buttonwood Park Zoo and Franklin Park Zoo before she joined the Attleboro facility.

The zoo highlighted her commitment to Reeves’ muntjacs, a small deer species native to Asia. St. George served as vice coordinator of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums program that manages the species’ population in accredited institutions, work that connects daily animal care with long-term conservation planning.

According to her family, St. George developed a migraine and numbness earlier this week. Doctors later found a clot near the base of her skull, and she died after a major stroke. Her family has asked that memorial donations be directed to Capron Park Zoo in place of flowers. The zoo said her loss is being felt by colleagues and the animals she cared for.
dek: The 39-year-old animal-care professional died after a stroke, leaving a record of work at several New England zoos and with a threatened deer species.
headline: Capron Park Zoo mourns zookeeper Kayla St. George

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Massachusetts judge denied a request to release Janette MacAusland and dismiss the criminal case accusing her of killing her two children in their Wellesley home.

MacAusland, 49, is charged with two counts of first-degree murder in the April deaths of her 7-year-old son and 6-year-old daughter. She has pleaded not guilty. Her attorney argued that the available record was insufficient to continue holding her, while prosecutors said they are still awaiting the medical examiner’s final determination of the children’s causes and manners of death.

The judge rejected the defense motion and ordered MacAusland to remain held without bail. Authorities previously alleged that she traveled to a relative’s home in Vermont after the children were found and made incriminating statements to police. Those allegations have not been tested at trial.

The case remains at a pretrial stage, and the ruling does not determine guilt. Prosecutors must prove each charge beyond a reasonable doubt, and MacAusland retains the presumption of innocence. Further court proceedings are expected after the medical examiner completes the outstanding findings.
dek: A judge denied the defense request to release Janette MacAusland and dismiss the case while prosecutors await final medical-examiner findings.
headline: Judge keeps Wellesley mother held without bail in children’s deaths

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Providence police arrested a 47-year-old man after a disturbance on Douglas Avenue in which a dog suffered a neck wound and required veterinary treatment.

Officers responded to 773 Douglas Avenue after receiving a report of a man armed with two knives, according to police information reported by NBC 10. Investigators said the man fled inside a residence while officers established contact. He later surrendered without a prolonged confrontation.

Police identified the suspect as Shah McKenney. The dog was taken to a veterinarian for treatment of a laceration to its neck; authorities had not released a detailed update on the animal’s condition at the time of the report.

McKenney faces two felony assault counts, malicious injury to an animal, disorderly conduct, obstruction and a charge involving prohibited weapons other than firearms. The charges reflect police allegations and have not been proven in court. The circumstances leading to the disturbance and the sequence in which the dog was injured remain part of the investigation.
dek: Police arrested a 47-year-old man after an armed disturbance on Douglas Avenue; an injured dog was taken for veterinary treatment.
headline: Providence man charged after dog injured during police disturbance

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Rhode Island Blood Center is using Childhood Cancer Awareness Month to remind residents that transfusions are a routine and often urgent part of treatment for many young cancer patients.

More than 15,000 children and adolescents are diagnosed with cancer in the United States each year, the center said. Chemotherapy, surgery and complications from treatment can create a need for red cells, platelets or plasma. The center estimates that more than 60% of people are eligible to donate blood, while only about 3% do so.

NBC 10 highlighted the family of Carrigan Nelson, who was diagnosed with osteosarcoma shortly after her 18th birthday. Her family said blood products helped extend her life during seven years of treatment before her death in 2025. They are encouraging eligible donors to give in her memory and for other patients.

A community back-to-school blood drive is scheduled for Monday, September 14, from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. at the Crowne Plaza in Warwick. Donor eligibility and appointment details are available from the Rhode Island Blood Center.
dek: The center says many young cancer patients depend on blood components and is promoting a September 14 community drive in Warwick.
headline: Rhode Island Blood Center urges donors during childhood cancer campaign

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Russian air strikes injured two people and started a fire in a nine-story apartment building in Kyiv early Friday, city authorities said.

Officials posted the preliminary account on Telegram after air-raid warnings urged residents to take shelter from drones. Emergency crews were responding to the residential fire, and authorities had not yet provided a full assessment of damage or whether additional people were trapped or displaced.

Separately, the governor of Russia’s Saratov region said Ukrainian drones damaged civilian infrastructure there but caused no casualties. Saratov is home to a Rosneft refinery as well as industrial and military facilities. The precise targets and extent of the damage were not immediately clear.

Reuters said it could not independently verify the battlefield accounts. Russia and Ukraine both deny deliberately targeting civilians, although residential areas and civilian infrastructure have repeatedly been damaged during the war. Casualty and damage figures may change as emergency teams complete searches and local authorities release additional information.
dek: Kyiv authorities reported a fire in a nine-story residential building after overnight air attacks, while Russia’s Saratov region reported infrastructure damage.
headline: Russian strikes injure two and ignite Kyiv apartment fire, officials say

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Hospitals and displaced families in Gaza are struggling to keep generators running as shortages of engine oil and replacement parts worsen an already severe electricity crisis.

At Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, one of four generators was out of service, Reuters reported. Staff were rotating power cuts to reduce the load on the remaining units, leaving patients who depend on ventilators, nebulizers and other powered equipment waiting for limited electricity.

Gaza has had no grid power since 2023, making generators central to hospitals, ambulances, water pumps and shelters. Médecins Sans Frontières warned that dwindling oil and parts threaten those services. Residents told Reuters that privately generated electricity now costs about 20 times its earlier price, putting it beyond the reach of many families.

Israel’s COGAT agency said a monitored mechanism facilitates the entry of equipment while seeking to prevent advanced items from reaching Hamas and to ensure supplies reach civilians. Aid groups say current access remains insufficient. With roughly two million people living largely in displacement sites, further generator failures could quickly interrupt medical and water services.
dek: Engine-oil and spare-parts shortages are forcing medical facilities to ration generator power while aid groups warn that essential services are at risk.
headline: Generator failures deepen power crisis at Gaza hospitals

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a package of 13 bills imposing new safeguards on social media platforms, artificial-intelligence chatbots and technology products used by children.

One measure bars platforms from exposing users under 16 to engagement features defined as psychologically exploitative, including infinite-scroll feeds and algorithmic autoplay. Another prohibits the manufacture and sale of toys containing AI companion chatbots for four years. Related provisions require parental controls and safety assessments for chatbot programs.

The package also expands criminal sanctions for child sexual abuse material to cover digitally altered or AI-generated depictions of minors. Newsom described the measures as the country’s broadest youth-technology protections, while supporters in both parties said existing safeguards had not kept pace with product design.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation criticized the social-media restrictions as a threat to privacy and free expression, illustrating the legal debate likely to follow implementation. California joins states including Utah, Texas, Florida and New York in regulating minors’ access to major platforms, but the details and enforcement models differ. Agencies must still define portions of the rules before the requirements take full effect.
dek: A 13-bill package restricts addictive platform features for users under 16, bars AI companion toys for four years and expands protections against synthetic abuse material.
headline: California enacts new child safeguards for social media and AI toys

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Micron Technology said its direct labor employees in Taiwan will receive fiscal-year rewards worth between 35 and 68 months of pay, an unusually large compensation package for workers in the island’s semiconductor sector.

Each eligible employee is guaranteed at least T$1.7 million, about $53,800, in cash compensation, Reuters reported. Workers who joined Micron before August 29, 2025, are also set to receive an additional T$1 million cash bonus. The exact award varies by employee and eligibility.

The announcement follows strong support among union members for possible strike action. Unions represent roughly two-thirds of Micron’s Taiwan workforce, making labor relations a significant operational issue for a company that depends on the island for memory-chip production.

Micron did not characterize the rewards as a settlement of the labor dispute in the Reuters report. The package nevertheless increases the financial incentive for skilled employees to remain with the company at a time when demand for advanced memory used in AI systems has tightened supply chains. Any effect on negotiations, staffing or production will depend on the unions’ next steps.
dek: The chipmaker announced large fiscal-year compensation packages for direct labor employees after unions showed strong support for possible strike action.
headline: Micron’s Taiwan workers receive rewards worth up to 68 months of pay

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Government bond yields rose sharply and Asian stocks fell Friday as surging oil prices and stronger U.S. producer inflation increased expectations that major central banks may keep policy tighter.

In early Asian trading reported by Reuters, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield reached 4.9708%, its highest level in about three years, while the 30-year yield rose to 5.3803%, a 19-year high. Futures markets put the chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase at roughly 70%. Those figures are snapshots from the article, not live quotes.

The selloff spread across regions. Japan’s Nikkei fell 2.8%, the CSI 300 dropped 1.2% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng declined 1.5%. Australian three-year yields reached a 15-year high, while Japan’s 10-year yield approached 3%.

Energy was the central pressure point: Brent crude had climbed nearly 13% for the week after Middle East disruptions intensified supply concerns. Higher fuel costs can feed inflation while reducing household and business spending, a combination that complicates central-bank decisions and weighs on both bonds and equities.
dek: Government debt sold off and Asian equities fell after rising energy prices and U.S. producer inflation pushed investors toward tighter-rate expectations.
headline: Global bond yields surge as oil shock revives rate-hike bets

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Oil futures extended their rally Friday and were on course for their first weekly finish above $100 a barrel since mid-May as conflict-related shipping risks tightened supply expectations.

At 00:45 GMT, Brent crude was quoted at $108.68 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate at $103.45, both about 1% higher in the Reuters report. Each benchmark had gained more than 6% Thursday and was up nearly 13% for the week. These are time-stamped market levels, not live prices.

The advance followed new disruptions around the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz, including the Houthi seizure of Yemen’s port city of Mocha and attacks affecting regional shipping. Rising transport and insurance costs are adding to concern about how much crude and refined fuel can move through key routes.

OPEC also cut its forecast for 2026 oil-demand growth to 380,000 barrels per day, its fifth consecutive downward revision, while reporting that August output fell by 640,000 barrels per day. The combination of reduced supply and weaker demand projections leaves prices highly sensitive to further military or shipping developments.
dek: Brent and U.S. crude extended gains after shipping and supply disruptions, while OPEC again lowered its 2026 demand-growth forecast.
headline: Oil benchmarks head for first $100-plus weekly finish since May

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Aryna Sabalenka defeated American Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2 to reach her fourth consecutive U.S. Open final and move within one victory of a third straight title in New York.

The world No. 1 recovered from a tightly contested opening set and took control with her serve and first-strike power. Sabalenka finished with 29 winners and seven aces, limiting Pegula’s opportunities to extend rallies and preventing the American from building momentum in the second set.

Sabalenka will face either Coco Gauff or Elena Rybakina in Saturday’s championship match. The matchup gives her another chance to reinforce a dominant recent run at Flushing Meadows after winning the previous two tournaments.

A victory would make Sabalenka the first woman since Serena Williams to win three consecutive U.S. Open singles titles. In the Open era, only Williams and Chris Evert have completed that streak. Pegula’s loss ends another deep run at her home major after she reached the semifinals for a third straight year.
dek: The world No. 1 advanced 7-5, 6-2 and will play for a third consecutive title at Flushing Meadows.
headline: Sabalenka beats Pegula to reach fourth straight U.S. Open final

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: LIV Golf received interim court approval to access $14 million in bankruptcy financing, giving the professional golf circuit near-term cash to continue operations during its Chapter 11 restructuring.

A federal bankruptcy judge in New Jersey approved the company’s first-day motions, including authority to pay wages, benefits and critical vendors. The interim amount is part of a proposed $49.6 million debtor-in-possession financing package backed by BC Partners Credit.

LIV filed for bankruptcy Tuesday after financial pressures left players and other creditors owed millions of dollars, according to court documents cited by Reuters. Chapter 11 allows a company to keep operating while it negotiates a plan to reorganize debts under court supervision.

The judge’s order is temporary and does not approve the full financing package or a final restructuring plan. A hearing on broader financing authority is scheduled for October 7. LIV has said it hopes to emerge from bankruptcy in early 2027, but that timeline will depend on creditor negotiations, court approval and the company’s ability to fund ongoing tournaments.
dek: A New Jersey court approved first-day Chapter 11 relief that lets the golf circuit continue paying employees and vendors while it reorganizes.
headline: LIV Golf wins interim access to $14 million in bankruptcy financing

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Loudon resident who survived the September 11 attack on the Pentagon is marking the tragedy’s 25th anniversary by preserving the memories of colleagues and urging younger generations not to let the day fade into abstraction.

John Donovan spent 22 years as a public-affairs officer at the Pentagon. He told the Concord Monitor that he was in a meeting when American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building on September 11, 2001. Donovan and coworkers escaped through a nearby corridor. He later learned that 35 people he knew through his work had died.

Donovan, who grew up in Concord, served in the Army during the Vietnam War and worked in journalism before reaching the Pentagon. He remained there until 2007, then returned to New Hampshire and continued participating in annual remembrance ceremonies.

His account will also appear in a forthcoming collection of survivor memories being assembled by two other military officers who lived through the attack. Donovan’s chapter focuses on the people he lost and on the public-affairs team’s return to work after the damaged section was rebuilt. The project adds a distinctly New Hampshire voice to the record of a day that killed 125 people inside the Pentagon.
dek: Retired public-affairs officer John Donovan is preserving memories of colleagues lost at the Pentagon and contributing to a forthcoming survivor history.
headline: Loudon Pentagon survivor marks 25 years since September 11

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A piece of Concord Public Library history has come home after 48,220 days: a bound magazine checked out in 1894 and returned this month by a Barrington resident who had kept it on a bookshelf for decades.

John Hanson told the Concord Monitor he did not know how the volume entered his family’s possession. The item is the September 1894 issue of “The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine,” still bearing the library’s markings and a one-week lending notice.

Hanson decided to return it after reading that the library had started a year-long freeze on overdue fines. By the Monitor’s calculation, the periodical would have accumulated $12,055 in penalties under a daily fine, although the library would not have charged him. Staff verified the date, issue number and bookplate to confirm that the copy had not simply been removed from circulation.

The library does not plan to lend the fragile magazine again. Instead, archivists hope to display it in the Concord Room, which houses local historical material. The episode gives the fine-free initiative an unusually tangible result and leaves staff with a mystery: who borrowed the magazine more than a century ago, and how it traveled from Concord to Hanson’s shelves.
dek: A Barrington man returned an 1894 magazine after spotting the library’s year-long fine freeze; archivists hope to display it in the Concord Room.
headline: Concord library receives book overdue by more than 132 years

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Oak Bluffs police are investigating a reported sexual assault at the Massachusetts State Police barracks on Martha’s Vineyard and have executed court-authorized search warrants at the facility.

The local department received the report in August, according to statements reported Thursday by NBC 10. Massachusetts State Police said the allegation involves two people who are not affiliated with the department. Authorities have not publicly identified either person or announced criminal charges.

Oak Bluffs Police Chief Jonathan Searle said his department has handled the case independently from State Police and followed its established investigative procedures. State Police said the agency is cooperating with the local inquiry and remains committed to pursuing justice in sexual-assault cases.

Oak Bluffs investigators are working with the Cape and Islands District Attorney’s Office. The agencies did not disclose what was sought or collected under the warrants, and the report did not describe the circumstances of the alleged assault. The inquiry remains active, meaning the reported allegation has not been tested in court. Officials have not announced a timetable for further information.
dek: Local officers executed court-authorized warrants at the Martha’s Vineyard facility while investigating an August report involving two people unaffiliated with State Police.
headline: Oak Bluffs police search state barracks in sexual-assault investigation

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial are describing the disagreement that led to a mistrial after roughly a week of deliberations over whether she was criminally responsible for the 2023 deaths of her three children in Duxbury.

Five jurors have now spoken to news organizations, NBC 10 reported. Three, including the foreperson, said one member of the panel would not join the others in finding Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity. Another juror said the panel’s vote shifted as members reviewed evidence before most of them reached the same position.
The public accounts are the jurors’ descriptions of closed deliberations; they are not new court findings. Clancy remains charged, and the mistrial did not resolve guilt or criminal responsibility.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has asked Judge William Sullivan to enter a not-guilty finding, arguing that prosecutors presented legally insufficient evidence of criminal responsibility. The defense is also pressing a double-jeopardy argument against another trial. A status conference is scheduled for September 29, when the judge is expected to consider the pending motions and the case’s next steps.
dek: Five panel members have spoken publicly after a week of deliberations failed to produce a unanimous decision on criminal responsibility.
headline: Jurors describe split that produced Lindsay Clancy mistrial

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Communities across Rhode Island will gather Friday to mark 25 years since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, with ceremonies scheduled from Exeter to Newport.

The day begins at 8:30 a.m. at the Rhode Island Veterans Cemetery Wall of Honor in Exeter. Warwick, East Providence and Central Falls have events set for 10 a.m., while West Greenwich plans a 10:28 a.m. observance on the Town Hall lawn. New England Institute of Technology will hold its annual ceremony at 11 a.m. in East Greenwich.

In Newport, a remembrance ceremony and wreath-laying are scheduled for noon at the U.S. Naval War College. The Rhode Island Fire Academy in Exeter will hold a separate service at 3:30 p.m. Public-safety departments, municipal officials and community groups are organizing many of the observances.

The statewide schedule reflects the anniversary’s continuing local resonance for families, first responders and military communities. Organizers advise attendees to verify event details before traveling because schedules may change. Similar services are planned across southeastern Massachusetts, including ceremonies in Attleboro, Fall River, Easton and Somerset.
dek: Observances across the state mark the attacks’ 25th anniversary with memorial services, wreath-laying and tributes led by public-safety agencies.
headline: Rhode Island communities hold September 11 remembrance ceremonies

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: North Kingstown-based REGENT has completed the first crewed flight of its Viceroy seaglider prototype on Narragansett Bay, moving the hybrid marine aircraft into the final stage of sea trials.

Two captains were aboard during the test, according to the company. REGENT said the prototype traveled 1,956 feet in ground-effect flight, reaching 33 feet above the water during a 30-second airborne segment.

The craft is designed to operate in three modes: floating from a dock, rising onto hydrofoils and then flying close to the water, where ground effect can reduce aerodynamic drag. REGENT is developing the platform for coastal passenger service, cargo transport and defense missions.

The milestone does not mean the vehicle is ready for commercial passengers. The company said continued testing will focus on refining performance, reducing operational risk and demonstrating readiness for future service. Even so, carrying crew through the full transition from waterborne operation to flight marks a substantial engineering step for a Rhode Island company building a new class of coastal transportation on Narragansett Bay.
dek: The North Kingstown company’s Viceroy prototype carried two captains in a brief ground-effect flight that begins the final stage of sea trials.
headline: REGENT seaglider completes first crewed flight on Narragansett Bay

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Hong Kong court sentenced two former leaders of the group that organized the city’s annual Tiananmen Square vigils to prison terms of at least seven years Friday, the latest major ruling under the territory’s national security law.

Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, received seven years, while Chow Hang-tung, 41, received seven years and three months after their convictions for inciting subversion. Both had pleaded not guilty and have been in custody since 2021, Reuters reported.

Albert Ho, 74, another former chairman of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, pleaded guilty in January and was sentenced to five years and two months. The court also imposed a HK$1.5 million fine on the alliance.

The group organized public commemorations of Beijing’s 1989 crackdown for years, when such gatherings were legal in Hong Kong. Those vigils were effectively halted after the security law took effect in 2020. The sentences are developing news because any appeals, defense responses or further court action had not been announced in the initial report.
dek: Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung were sentenced under the national security law after convictions tied to a disbanded group’s pro-democracy activities.
headline: Hong Kong court gives Tiananmen vigil leaders seven-year terms

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Commercial vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell into single digits Thursday, according to preliminary ship-tracking data that underscores how sharply war and shipping restrictions have disrupted one of the world’s most important energy corridors.

Kpler recorded seven transits, down from 11 Wednesday and below the recent 10-day average of 15, Reuters reported. Five vessels entered the strait and two exited. The tracked cargoes included fertilizer, grain, steel, dry bulk material and petroleum products.

The count may not capture vessels traveling with Automatic Identification System transponders switched off. Before the Iran war began February 28, roughly 125 large commercial ships typically passed through the strait each day, carrying a significant share of global crude-oil and liquefied-natural-gas supplies.

Traffic data can change as tracking services receive new signals, so the Thursday count remains preliminary. Still, the decline adds a fresh measure of stress on maritime trade as a U.S. blockade has halted Iranian crude exports and instability has spread to nearby routes. Traders, shippers and consumers are watching the corridor for further restrictions or attacks.
dek: Preliminary Kpler data recorded sharply fewer commercial crossings Thursday than the recent average as war and shipping restrictions squeeze a critical energy route.
headline: Hormuz vessel traffic falls to seven transits, tracking data shows

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: China’s industry ministry has set a 2030 goal for large-scale deployment of autonomous vehicles, pairing expansion plans with tighter oversight of vehicle production, road safety and software updates.

The roadmap calls for automated driving on highways, urban expressways and selected city streets. It also aims to produce multiple Chinese automakers ranked among the world’s top 10 by sales and to increase the global influence of Chinese brands and technical standards.

Safety is central to the plan: the ministry wants autonomous vehicles to achieve better safety performance than human drivers. Regulators also intend to create special approval pathways for some components and low-volume vehicles while strengthening antitrust enforcement and product-quality supervision.

The document addresses the industry’s capacity problem as well as its technology ambitions. Officials plan to discourage overinvestment, eliminate inefficient production and encourage consolidation across automakers and battery manufacturers. China also wants deeper research and investment partnerships with foreign companies. The roadmap sets policy direction, but broad deployment will still depend on technical validation, local road approvals and enforcement of the new rules.
dek: A new industry roadmap calls for self-driving systems on highways, urban expressways and selected city roads while tightening safety and software rules.
headline: China targets large-scale autonomous-vehicle deployment by 2030

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Microsoft plans to expand its global data-center capacity to about 38 gigawatts by 2032, more than triple its current footprint, Bloomberg News reported Thursday through people familiar with the plans.

The company now operates about 12 gigawatts of capacity, according to the report, but only about 2 gigawatts is dedicated to AI-specific chips. Roughly one-third of the planned 38-gigawatt total is expected to serve specialized AI hardware. Microsoft did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.

The scale reflects the computing and electricity demands of generative-AI products such as Copilot and ChatGPT. Microsoft has forecast $50 billion in capital spending for its fiscal first quarter of 2027 and $175 billion for calendar 2026.
