Anthropic did not identify the users or say they were members of the armed group, so the attribution is based on location and the activity the company observed.

The accounts sought assistance involving hypersonic missiles and guided warheads. Anthropic said the effort appeared unsuccessful: after a failed rocket test, the users returned to Claude with questions about what had gone wrong. They had nonetheless assembled an offline simulation toolkit before Anthropic detected and blocked the activity.

The episode illustrates how general-purpose AI can lower the barrier to organizing complex technical work even when it does not produce a functioning weapon. Anthropic said it shared its findings with public- and private-sector partners. The disclosure arrives as the Houthis expand their regional reach and as AI developers face pressure to demonstrate that monitoring systems can identify high-risk military and dual-use requests.
dek: The company said accounts in Houthi-held territory tried to develop missile technology but appeared unsuccessful and were blocked.
headline: Anthropic says Yemen-based users sought advanced weapons help from Claude

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts lawmakers are considering new limits on automated license-plate readers as municipalities reconsider contracts with Flock Safety and residents raise privacy concerns. The ACLU of Massachusetts says 25 communities have canceled contracts or ended pilot programs during the past 18 months.

A bill filed by Watertown Rep. Steve Owens would establish driver-privacy rules for law-enforcement use of plate-reader data. A legislative summary says it would generally require a warrant to access data held by another entity, cap routine retention at 14 days and prohibit government use of the systems to monitor constitutionally protected activity. House members of the Transportation Committee endorsed the measure 11-0 in March, but it remains before Ways and Means.

The debate intensified after a Suffolk Superior Court judge ordered State Police to release camera-location records and audit logs sought by the ACLU. State Police says fewer than 2% of department members can query its system and that searches require training, a case reference and documented purpose. Flock says it supports privacy and accountability guardrails while preserving legitimate public-safety uses.
dek: A pending bill would limit data retention and require warrants for some outside database access as communities reconsider Flock contracts.
headline: Massachusetts lawmakers weigh guardrails for license-plate readers
sourceName: NBC10 Boston / State House News Service

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A sustained increase in energy prices could begin to weigh on household consumption in the euro zone by autumn, European Central Bank Chief Economist Philip Lane said Friday. Speaking at a conference in Ireland, Lane emphasized that the effect depends on whether the current rise persists.

The warning puts household demand at the center of the energy shock facing Europe. Higher power and fuel bills can leave consumers with less money for other purchases, while also complicating the inflation outlook that guides interest-rate decisions. Lane did not announce a policy change or provide a new forecast, describing the issue instead as a continuing source of uncertainty.

For markets, the comment highlights the two-sided challenge confronting the ECB: energy costs can lift inflation even as they weaken growth by reducing spending. Investors will therefore be watching incoming consumption and price data for evidence of which effect is becoming stronger. Lane’s remarks were made before new autumn data are available, so they are a risk assessment rather than a conclusion that demand has already declined.
dek: The central bank’s chief economist said the duration of higher energy costs remains an important uncertainty for euro-zone households and policymakers.
headline: ECB’s Lane says persistent energy rise could hit autumn consumption

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Reserve Bank of India has rejected Tata Sons’ request to deregister as a non-bank lender, according to two people familiar with the decision. The outcome leaves the closely held parent of several major Indian companies nearer to a possible stock-market listing.

Tata Sons had asked to give up its classification as a core investment company. RBI rules can require non-bank lenders with assets above 1 trillion rupees, or access to public funds, to list. Tata Sons reported standalone assets of 1.75 trillion rupees as of March 2025. The central bank communicated its decision in a letter Saturday, the sources said.

The holding company controls businesses including Tata Consultancy Services, Tata Motors, Tata Steel and Air India, and has sought to remain private. Listing pressure has also come from Shapoorji Pallonji Group, its second-largest shareholder. Tata Trusts owns 66% of Tata Sons. The RBI, Tata Sons and Tata Trusts did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and no listing timetable has been announced.
dek: India’s central bank rejected the holding company’s bid to shed its non-bank lender registration, according to two sources.
headline: RBI rejection moves Tata Sons closer to potential public listing

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Lando Norris secured pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix on Saturday with a late lap at Madrid’s new Madring circuit. The McLaren driver recorded 1 minute, 31.824 seconds and beat Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli by 0.011 seconds.

Norris sat sixth before his final attempt but found enough speed despite acknowledging a small error at the last corner. The result delivered the 19th pole of his Formula One career and his third of the 2026 season. Max Verstappen qualified third for Red Bull, while Lewis Hamilton placed fourth.

Starting position could carry extra weight at a circuit where drivers and teams expect overtaking to be difficult. The narrow qualifying margin also leaves little separation among the leading cars before Sunday’s race. Madring is hosting Formula One for the first time, adding an unfamiliar layout to the normal challenge of managing tires, strategy and traffic. Norris now has the best starting spot, but Antonelli and Verstappen will begin close enough to apply immediate pressure.
dek: The McLaren driver edged Kimi Antonelli by 0.011 seconds with a late qualifying lap at Formula One’s new Madrid circuit.
headline: Lando Norris takes Spanish Grand Prix pole at Madring

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: American sailor Charlotte Rose won the ILCA 6 Women’s World Championship on Saturday after navigating two final races in difficult conditions on Dublin Bay. Rose carried 15 points from qualifying and finished second and sixth in the medal-deciding series to end the regatta with 23 points.

Belgium’s two-time world champion Emma Plasschaert finished second with 28 points, while Denmark’s Anna Munch took third with 34. Rose became the first non-European to win the title in 20 years, following China’s Xu Lijia in 2006. The ILCA 6 is the women’s single-handed dinghy class used in Olympic competition.

Rose celebrated by deliberately capsizing her boat and jumping into the water after the result was confirmed. Her consistency proved decisive in a final contested by 10 boats, where changing conditions placed a premium on minimizing poor finishes. The championship adds a major global title for U.S. sailing and gives Rose a benchmark result in one of the sport’s most competitive individual classes.
dek: The American sailor finished with 23 points to become the first non-European women’s champion in the Olympic dinghy class since 2006.
headline: Charlotte Rose wins ILCA 6 world title in Dublin Bay

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Merrimack County judge is considering a lawsuit seeking to remove a proposed New Hampshire school tax cap from the November ballot. Superior Court Judge Dan St. Hilaire heard arguments over whether the question gives voters a clear explanation of the change they are being asked to approve.

The challenge was brought by Campton school board member Kelly Wieser and Warner taxpayer David Bates. They contend the wording is confusing and does not adequately describe how the cap would operate. The state argues that lawmakers properly enacted the measure and that the plaintiffs do not have legal standing to block it.

If approved by voters, the proposal would limit annual growth in local property-tax levies for schools, with adjustments tied to inflation and new construction. It would also place a 6% limit on growth in school administrative-unit central-office spending. Timing is tight because ballot printing is expected to begin late next week. St. Hilaire indicated that a decision would come quickly, giving election officials and local governments little room for delay before ballots are finalized.
dek: A superior court judge is expected to rule quickly as ballot printing approaches for the proposed school spending and tax limits.
headline: Judge weighs challenge to New Hampshire school tax-cap ballot question

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan has joined election officials from five other Republican-led states in asking the U.S. Supreme Court to keep new federal mail-ballot rules from taking effect during the 2026 election. Their filing focuses on the disruption that late procedural changes could create, not on the underlying policy dispute.

The officials represent New Hampshire, Kentucky, North Dakota, South Dakota, Georgia and Kansas. They argue that election administrators are already carrying out the midterm calendar and that new requirements could confuse voters and local officials. Some absentee ballots have already been issued, while federal law requires ballots for military and overseas voters to be sent by September 19.

The dispute follows a March executive order and related U.S. Postal Service rules. The proposed changes include sharing voter information with the Postal Service and procedures that officials say could cause mailed ballots to be rejected over processing errors. A federal court in Massachusetts blocked part of the rules, prompting the administration to seek Supreme Court intervention. The state officials told the court they were taking no position on the rules’ legality or goals while urging stability this close to voting.
dek: David Scanlan and election officials from five other states say late federal changes could disrupt voting already underway.
headline: New Hampshire joins states seeking pause on new mail-ballot rules

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts has offered Insulet a potential incentive package worth more than $40 million as the medical-device maker considers a substantial expansion in Acton. The package would provide at least $40,000 in state tax credits for each qualifying new job, covering as many as 1,000 net full-time positions created through 2032.

Insulet, which makes the Omnipod insulin-delivery system, is headquartered in Acton and employs about 1,700 people in Massachusetts. The company has added roughly 200 employees in the state this year. Its preliminary plans include a $33 million renovation at 35 Nagog Park for approximately 500 to 530 workers, along with another $11 million to $12 million investment at 100 Nagog Park.

The offer is the largest single-company award in the history of the Massachusetts life-sciences tax incentive program, according to the report. Insulet has not made a final decision on the expansion, so the jobs and construction remain contingent on the company moving ahead and meeting the program’s requirements. The proposal reflects the state’s effort to retain growing life-sciences manufacturers while tying public support to job creation over several years.
dek: The medical-device maker is considering two Nagog Park investments and as many as 1,000 additional Massachusetts jobs through 2032.
headline: Massachusetts offers Insulet more than $40 million for Acton expansion

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Construction is underway to convert the former St. Augustine’s Convent and Paraclete Center in South Boston into affordable housing for older adults. The $15.7 million McDevitt Senior Homes project will create 35 income-restricted apartments and one manager’s unit in the historic building.

The approximately 31,000-square-foot development combines restoration of the existing structure with a five-story rear addition. Plans call for preserving recognizable architectural features while adapting the interior for accessible residences and common areas. The project is intended to add senior housing without removing the property’s long-standing neighborhood identity.

Public financing includes $5.145 million from the City of Boston and Community Preservation Act funds, plus $850,000 from the Federal Home Loan Bank of Boston. Construction began in July, and project partners held a formal groundbreaking on August 20. The reuse adds a relatively small but targeted supply of below-market homes in a city where older residents can face steep housing costs and limited accessible options. Work will now move through the renovation and new-construction phases before residents can occupy the building.
dek: The $15.7 million adaptive-reuse project will preserve the historic property while adding income-restricted apartments for older adults.
headline: Former South Boston convent begins conversion to 35 affordable senior homes

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Tiverton returned to varsity football as the first regular-season Friday night brought a full slate of high school games across Southern New England. Sports Team 10’s Week 1 roundup featured action from nine matchups involving Rhode Island and nearby Massachusetts programs.

The schedule included Johnston and East Providence, Davies and Lincoln, Saint Raphael and Cumberland, Barrington and Burrillville, and Tiverton and Smithfield. Classical, Woonsocket, Mount Pleasant, Coventry, Attleboro, Seekonk and Old Colony were also represented in the evening’s coverage. The broad opening-night card gave teams their first meaningful test after preseason preparation.

Tiverton’s return was a notable part of the night because it restored another local program to the statewide football calendar. Week 1 results are only an early measure, but opening games begin to establish rotations, identify areas for improvement and shape divisional races. The Friday slate also restored the familiar rhythm of community football under the lights, with multiple schools beginning campaigns at the same time across the region. Teams now turn quickly toward film review and their second-week opponents.
dek: Nine matchups opened the regular-season Friday-night schedule, with Tiverton’s return highlighting the Southern New England slate.
headline: Tiverton returns as Southern New England football opens Week 1

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A new national maternal-health report is prompting questions about how consistently Rhode Island families receive support from pregnancy through the postpartum period. The Harris Poll and digital maternal-health company Babyscripts focused on whether patients feel heard, can obtain help and remain connected to care after delivery.

RINewsToday used the findings to examine gaps that can persist even when a patient asks for assistance. The report emphasizes continuity across the full maternal-care timeline, rather than treating childbirth as the end of routine support. It also highlights the importance of clear follow-up, accessible treatment pathways and communication between patients and clinicians.

The findings do not provide a Rhode Island-specific performance score, but they offer practical questions for the state’s hospitals, insurers and public-health agencies. Those include how quickly postpartum concerns are assessed, whether referrals lead to actual appointments and how families are supported between scheduled visits. The local relevance is especially clear for mental-health concerns, which may emerge or intensify after a family leaves the hospital. The report’s central message is that asking for help should begin a reliable care process, not leave patients to navigate disconnected services alone.
dek: A Harris Poll and Babyscripts report is prompting local questions about follow-up, access and continuity after childbirth.
headline: Maternal-care report highlights postpartum support gaps for Rhode Island

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Russian attacks killed at least six people and injured dozens across Ukraine on Saturday, according to regional officials. Two people were killed when a strike hit a grocery store in the Zhytomyr region, while two deaths were reported around Zaporizhzhia and two more in Kryvyi Rih.

Officials said 11 people were injured in Zaporizhzhia and nearby communities. In Odesa, 37 people were reported hurt, including an infant, and two people remained missing. The casualty reports were still developing as emergency crews worked at multiple damaged sites.

Russia said its forces struck port facilities, ships and industrial plants. Ukraine separately said it hit a synthetic-rubber plant in the Russian city of Togliatti. Reuters said it could not independently verify the battlefield claims from either side. The attacks extended the war’s pressure on civilian areas and infrastructure, with casualty counts subject to revision as rescue operations continue. The geographic spread—from central and southern regions to Odesa on the Black Sea—underscored the scale of the latest exchange and the need to distinguish official claims from independently confirmed damage.
dek: Regional officials reported deaths in Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, while 37 people were injured in Odesa.
headline: Russian strikes kill six and injure dozens across Ukraine

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The confirmed death toll from a ferry fire in the Philippines rose to 76 on Saturday after responders recovered 41 additional charred remains, authorities said. Thirteen people were still unaccounted for, while 43 survivors had been confirmed from the vessel carrying more than 130 people.

Rescue teams entered the ferry on Friday after the fire was extinguished and found many of the remains in the economy passenger section. The Maritime Industry Authority said survivors reported hearing two explosions, but investigators have not established what started the blaze. Identification work is continuing alongside the search for those still missing.

The new toll is a substantial increase from earlier reports and may change again as recovery teams complete their work. Authorities are also reviewing the passenger count and the sequence of events aboard the vessel. The disaster has shifted from an active rescue toward recovery, identification and investigation, though families are still waiting for definitive information. Officials have not announced a final cause. Until the inquiry is complete, reports about explosions describe witness accounts rather than a determination of why the fire spread.
dek: Responders recovered 41 additional remains as identification work continued and 13 people remained unaccounted for.
headline: Philippine ferry-fire death toll rises to 76

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Financial technology company Revolut confirmed that sensitive customer information was disclosed after fraudulent data requests arrived from an email domain belonging to a legitimate government agency. The company said the requests were not authentic, even though they appeared to come through an official channel.

The exposed information included birth dates, contact details and identity documents such as passports and driver’s licenses, according to TechCrunch reporting cited by Reuters. Revolut did not disclose how many customers were affected. It said its own systems and customer funds were not compromised.

Revolut blocked the address used in the requests and notified the agency, law enforcement and regulators. The incident illustrates a difficult security problem for companies that regularly respond to lawful government requests: attackers may exploit trust in a real agency’s infrastructure without directly breaking into the company holding the customer data. That makes verification of the requester, not only the message’s domain, a critical control. Customers affected by an identity-document leak may face longer-term fraud risks even when accounts and balances remain secure, because exposed credentials can be reused in later impersonation attempts.
dek: The fintech said its systems and customer funds were unaffected, but identity and contact records were disclosed through fraudulent requests.
headline: Revolut confirms customer-data leak after spoofed government requests

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Reuters and video platform CuttingRoom announced an integration designed to let newsrooms search, edit and publish Reuters footage through an AI-assisted browser workflow. The partnership connects Reuters’ Model Context Protocol server with CuttingRoom’s ShortCut editing system.

Editors can use plain-language instructions to find relevant clips and perform production tasks including cuts, audio mixing, color correction, captions and platform-specific formatting. Reuters material can be placed on the same timeline as a newsroom’s own video, reducing the need to move files among separate tools during production.

The companies said each newsroom retains control over its data and can configure editorial rules for the AI workflow. That governance layer matters because faster editing does not remove the need for source verification, rights management or human review before publication. The integration is aimed at repetitive production work around trusted footage rather than automated reporting without oversight. For publishers, the practical test will be whether the system can shorten turnaround time while consistently preserving context, attribution and house standards across broadcast, web and social formats.
dek: The integration connects verified Reuters footage with CuttingRoom’s browser editor and plain-language production tools.
headline: Reuters and CuttingRoom launch AI-assisted newsroom video workflow

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Investors are preparing for a Federal Reserve meeting in which a rate increase remains a meaningful possibility, a sharp change from the easing expectations that dominated earlier in the cycle. The decision is due Wednesday and follows inflation data that kept pressure on policymakers to contain price growth.

The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield has approached the 5% threshold, raising borrowing costs across mortgages, corporate debt and other credit markets. Higher yields can also challenge stock valuations because future earnings are discounted at a steeper rate. Reuters reported that market pricing leaned toward an increase, though the final decision and the Fed’s guidance remained uncertain.

The S&P 500 was still up about 12% for the year at the time of the report, leaving investors to weigh strong equity performance against tighter financial conditions. Attention will extend beyond the rate itself to the central bank’s projections and explanation of how it views persistent inflation, labor conditions and growth. Because the meeting has not occurred, current market positioning is an expectation rather than confirmation of a policy move.
dek: Bond yields near 5% and persistent inflation have raised the stakes for Wednesday’s central-bank decision.
headline: Investors brace for a possible Federal Reserve rate hike

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: London equities recovered on Friday as crude oil retreated, but the rebound was not enough to prevent a difficult week for major British indexes. The FTSE 100 and the domestically focused FTSE 250 each closed about 0.4% higher for the session.

Banks helped lead the recovery, with HSBC up 1.5% and Barclays gaining 1.9% in the reported session. Construction and materials shares rose about 1.8%. Softer oil prices provided some relief after energy costs had added to concern about inflation and the path of interest rates.

Despite Friday’s gain, the FTSE 100 recorded its largest weekly decline since late July, while the FTSE 250 posted its steepest weekly loss in more than four months. Traders were pricing roughly 44 basis points of Bank of England rate increases by year-end at the time of the report. Those figures describe Friday’s close and contemporaneous expectations, not live prices. The split between a positive final session and a negative week shows how energy markets and rate assumptions continued to drive short-term sentiment across British shares.
dek: The FTSE 100 and FTSE 250 each added 0.4% Friday, yet both finished a volatile week with substantial declines.
headline: London shares rebound Friday but post steep weekly losses

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Christian Harrison and Neal Skupski won the U.S. Open men’s doubles championship on Saturday, defeating Germany’s Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz 6-4, 7-6 (6). The title gave the American-British partnership its second Grand Slam trophy of the season after winning the Australian Open.

Harrison and Skupski controlled the opening set, then closed a tighter second set in a tiebreak. Their ability to finish in straight sets limited the opportunity for Krawietz and Puetz to force a deciding third set on the New York hard courts.

The victory completes a notable two-major season for a pairing that has translated complementary serving and net play into results on different surfaces and continents. Grand Slam doubles matches often turn on a small number of return points and quick exchanges, making the second-set tiebreak the decisive pressure moment. Harrison and Skupski handled it to secure the championship without extending the match. The result also places them among the season’s most successful men’s doubles teams, with major titles at both the first and final Grand Slam events of 2026.
dek: The American-British pair beat Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz in straight sets for its second major title of 2026.
headline: Harrison and Skupski win U.S. Open men’s doubles title

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Jakob Ingebrigtsen withdrew from Sunday’s 1,500-meter race at the Ultimate Championship, postponing another anticipated meeting with British rival Josh Kerr. The Norwegian runner had won the 5,000 meters on Friday but decided against racing twice within three days as he continues his recovery from Achilles surgery.

Ingebrigtsen underwent the operation in February and returned to competition last month after nearly a year away. His Friday victory showed that he could again handle championship-level racing, but the shorter turnaround presented a different recovery demand. The withdrawal leaves the 1,500 without one of its highest-profile entrants.

The decision also delays a rivalry that has become one of middle-distance running’s central storylines. Ingebrigtsen and Kerr have not raced each other since 2024, and their tactical contrast makes each scheduled meeting a major event. For Ingebrigtsen, the choice prioritizes a controlled return over adding another race immediately after the 5,000. Kerr remains in the field, while the Norwegian’s next chance to test himself over 1,500 meters will depend on his recovery and schedule.
dek: The Norwegian runner cited recovery demands after winning Friday’s 5,000 meters during his return from Achilles surgery.
headline: Ingebrigtsen withdraws from 1,500 meters, delaying Kerr showdown
